items.title: The free closure of an induction: where free steps come to rest
items.text:
The steps that cost mibz2 no bookkeeping can be taken in any order and still meet at one end point, now proved to belong to the block itself.

15 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 1. What does one step do?
items.text:
Suppose you want to compress the four bytes abac. Their four rotations, sorted, are abac, acab, baca and caba, so the last column is cbaa. It has three runs, c, b and aa, so the rebuild starts with three letters. Call them Y, Z and X:

Letter Its rows (top) LF sends them to (bottom) Word Y, the run c row 0 row 3 c Z, the run b row 1 row 2 b X, the run aa rows 2–3 rows 0–1 a

The figure draws each letter twice. The top strip shows where its rows sit in the last column. The bottom strip shows where LF sends them, and the shaded band joins the two. The numbers above the strips count boundaries between rows, so boundary 4 is the end of row 3.

One free step on the column of abac

Before: X and Y end at boundary 401234topbottomY · cY · cZ · bZ · bX · aX · aAfter the step at 4: row 3 is cut01234topbottomcutcutY · acY · acZ · bZ · bX · aX · a Computed by a program that steps the column exactly as the checker in section 4 does; not drawn by hand. Top strip: each letter’s rows. Bottom strip: where LF sends them. Each box shows the letter and its word. Grey boxes are rows the step has cut.

Two things end at boundary 4. In the top strip, X's rows 2–3 end there. In the bottom strip, so does Y's landing place, row 3. That makes boundary 4 a coincidence, and a step can be taken there. Y's one row lands on row 3. Row 3 belongs to X, which sends it on to row 1. So row 3 is only a stopover on Y's way. The step cuts row 3 out, and Y now jumps from row 0 straight to row 1. Its jump reads c and then a. LF runs backwards through the text, so in text order its word grows at the front: c becomes ac, which is indeed in abac. X loses the row, and keeps row 2, which still goes to row 0.

The step is free because of where Y now lands. Its new landing place starts a boundary at 1 in the bottom strip. The top strip already had a boundary at 1, between Y's row and Z's. So the step erased the boundary at 4 and created none that wasn't already there. A step that is not free, a paid step, would put a boundary at a new place, and some later step would have to remove it. A step between two letters of the same length is always free, since one letter simply takes over the other's place.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 2. Does the order matter?
items.text:
The column has a second free step available at the start. At boundary 2, Z's row 1 ends in the top strip. X's landing place, rows 0–1, ends there in the bottom strip. Here Z is the shorter piece, so row 1 is cut. X's row 3 used to land on row 1 and go on with Z to row 2. Now it jumps straight to row 2. That one row splits off from X and becomes Z, with the word ba.

Both steps are free, and they share a letter: X. Each one changes X's length, so neither leaves the other's starting point untouched. The figure takes them in both orders.

Two free steps, two orders, one state

Start: free steps at 2 and 401234Y·cY·cZ·bZ·bX·aX·aStep at 4 firstY·ac; X shrinks01234cutcutY·acY·acZ·bZ·bX·aX·aStep at 2 firstZ·ba; X shrinks01234cutcutY·cY·cX·aX·aZ·baZ·baEither order: one staterows 1 and 3 cut01234cutcutcutcutY·bacY·bacX·aX·astep at 4step at 2then at 2then at 4In each state: upper strip top, lower strip bottom Computed, as in the figure above. Green lines mark the free steps available in each state. Taking the step at 4 first and then the one at 2, or the other way round, gives the same letters, places and words: X at row 2 with the word a, and Y at row 0, landing on row 2, with the word bac.

The left path makes Y's word ac first, and then the step at 2 puts b in front of it. The right path makes Z's word ba first, and then the step at 4 hands Y the whole of ba followed by its own c. Either way, Y ends with bac and X with a. In the language of rewriting systems this is a diamond, or a square. Two steps leave one state, and one step on each side brings them back together.

The tiny block goes on to its end. After the diamond, X and Y form a cycle of two letters, each landing on the other's rows, and one more free step closes it whole. A program tried every one of the twelve orders in which the free steps of cbaa can be taken. All twelve take three steps. Each ends with one letter whose word is abac, acab, baca or caba: the same cycle, read from different starting points. That is the exception in the theorem. On a four-byte block the whole text closes during the free steps. On the Wikidata blocks, where the free steps stop at about a fifth of the runs, none did. bzip2 stores with every block the row of the original rotation, which says where to start reading in any case.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 3. Why does it hold for every block?
items.text:
Two diamonds on one example prove nothing in general, so the proof goes through a classical result. Newman's lemma, from 1942, says that a system of rewriting steps has a single end point from every start if two things hold.

  1. Termination. No sequence of steps goes on forever. Each free step erases one boundary and creates none, and a block has only finitely many boundaries, so this holds.
  2. Local confluence. Whenever two steps are available in the same state, there is some way to continue from each of them so that both reach the same state again.

Termination is what lets the second, local condition decide the global answer. Without it, two paths could keep diverging forever, each step of the way looking reconcilable.

So the proof takes any two free steps available together, at boundaries c₁ and c₂, and shows that they can be brought back together. It rests on two facts. First, a free step touches only its own two letters, and removes no boundary but its own. Second, the place where a free step's shorter letter lands always lies strictly inside the longer letter's interval, so it can never be the other step's coincidence. Then two steps relate in exactly one of four ways:

  1. No letter in common. Neither step changes anything the other reads, so each stays free after the other, and the two orders give the same state.
  2. One shared letter X, whose rows end at c₁ and whose landing place ends at c₂. This is the case of abac, and the hard one. Each step can be one of three kinds: the letter above wins (it is longer), the letter below wins, or the two are equal. That gives nine combinations of kinds for the pair. The table below shows which can happen.
  3. One shared letter, the other way round. This is case 2 with the steps' names swapped.
  4. Both letters shared. The two letters form a cycle of two, and either step closes it. The two results differ only in where the closed letter lies and in which rotation of its word it holds. That is where the theorem's exception comes from.

In case 2, X is the upper letter at c₁, over Y, and the lower letter at c₂, under Z. Rows compare X with Y at c₁, and columns compare X with Z at c₂:

At c₁ ↓ / at c₂ → Z longer X longer equal X longer than Y impossible square; Y and Z equal impossible Y longer than X square impossible square equal square impossible square

The four impossible combinations fail for one reason. For both steps to be free, one of them would have to land strictly inside a letter's interval in the other strip, where no boundary can be. The five squares are each written out in both orders in the proof, and each reaches the same letters, places and words. abac is the square in the top row. X has two rows, so it is longer than Y and longer than Z. Y and Z have one row each, as forced.

A last detail settles the step count. Every square closes with one step on each side, and the closing cycles of case 4 need none. So any two complete paths of free steps have the same length, not only the same end point.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 4. How was it checked?
items.text:
The proof was checked against a program that steps every short column exhaustively. It covers every column over 2 letters up to length 14, and likewise over 3, 4 and 5 letters up to lengths 9, 7 and 6. On each column it follows three random complete paths of free steps. At every state along every path, it takes every ordered pair of free steps available, classifies it by case and kinds, and runs both orders. It checks that the two orders reach the same state. In case 4 it checks instead that one step closes a cycle, and that the two agree up to its rotation.

The results, over 10.7 million ordered pairs. Same state counts the pairs whose two orders reach the same state, and closed cycle the case 4 pairs that agree up to rotation:

Alphabet, longest Pairs Same state Closed cycle (case 4) Exceptions 2 letters, 14 4,322,196 4,042,698 279,498 0 3 letters, 9 3,434,430 3,129,050 305,380 0 4 letters, 7 1,741,700 1,531,570 210,130 0 5 letters, 6 1,164,480 991,358 173,122 0

In every alphabet, the combinations of kinds that occur are exactly the ones the proof allows. Case 2 shows its five squares, and case 3 their mirror images. Case 4 shows only the three combinations that close a cycle. None of the four impossible combinations was ever seen. Rerun for this post, the program gives the same counts.

Before the proof, a separate count had run the free steps to the end under different orders and compared the results directly. No two orders ever disagreed, on 404,677 short columns under ten orders each, or on the 233 Wikidata blocks and four blocks of prose. On every real block the results were equal exactly, with no closed cycle to allow for.

items.title: 5. What is proved and what is counted
items.text:
The research record labels each statement as proved by hand, or counted (exact for the data it ran on, but no more). For this result:

  • Proved: free steps in any order reach one end point, up to closed cycles. A program checked every case on 10.7 million pairs of steps.
  • Proved: every complete path of free steps has the same number of steps.
  • Proved: after the free closure, no step adds a letter.
  • Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks under three orders: before reaching the closure, free-first orders never held more long words than the closure has letters.
  • Counted, on all 233 Wikidata blocks: the closure leaves 0.185 r letters and takes 0.896 r steps, at the median.

The two counted figures are now properties of each block, so their spread across blocks is a spread across text, not across algorithms. The Wikidata corpus is an extract of a Wikidata dump. Its blocks here are the 233 with at least 65,536 rows, and each figure is divided by that block's own r.

items.title: 6. What could a decoder do with it?
items.text:
Everything in this section is a consequence of the theorem, not a measurement.

Any order is correct. The cost of a free-first decoder is in finding its free steps. It needs a worklist of ready steps. An earlier count priced that worklist at about 150 instructions a run on one thread, against 115 for Cells' sweep from the right-hand end. The theorem says a decoder may take its free steps in whatever order its worklist yields them: a stack, a sweep, or batches. The end point, the step count and the bound on width hold for all of them. So a worklist can be designed for speed alone.

Splitting one block between threads. Two free steps on different letters commute. So free steps can be handed to different threads, and they reach the same state as on one thread. The condition is that each thread's step writes only its own two letters' records. That is a way to split one block's rebuild that is proved correct, which matters for how mibz2 uses many cores. It decodes blocks in parallel either with each thread on a block of its own, or with teams of threads sharing a block. On a 10-core Intel desktop at ten threads, a block per thread took 1.040 times the teams' wall time in the latest run. Its 95% interval is 1.019 to 1.061 (the run's report). The working explanation, not yet measured directly, is that each thread's live state competes for the shared cache. A smaller live state, and a proved way to share one block's free steps, both bear on that.

A bound fixed by the block. After the closure, no step adds a letter. So from the closure on, a decoder that takes free steps first never needs more live letters than the closure has. That is about 0.19 r on Wikidata, against the r slots Cells reserves today. Before the closure, the bound held on every block counted.

No free-first decoder has been built. A first decoder that keeps the untouched one-byte letters implicit, and writes a letter only when its word first grows, has been built with Cells' right-end order and is being measured. None of it has been timed yet.
path: The free closure of an induction

items.title: 7. What is still open?
items.text:
Which steps does the closure leave? Only equal steps remove letters, and a block's rebuild makes exactly r − 1 of them. So the closure's letter count is 1 plus the number of equal steps that can only become ready after a paid step. Saying which equal steps those are, from the block's runs, would describe the closure without running it. That is the next question.

One block on many cores, by rounds. A different route also reaches the end of a rebuild: repeatedly cut the map down to the rows where runs branch, all at once. It collapses a whole Wikidata block to between 2 and 560 letters in 5 to 18 such rounds, and the work within a round is independent. Cells' right-end order, by contrast, has a chain of 93 dependent rounds at the median. As counted, though, each round walks every row it removes, so its work grows with the rows rather than the runs, which is the cost Cells exists to avoid. Whether a round can be computed on letters and their words alone has not been tested.

Is width a cutwidth? The width post links width to the cutwidth of a graph: line up its vertices, cut between any two, and count the edges that cross. Whether the width of a rebuild is exactly a cutwidth of the block's cycle of rows, bundled by runs, is a conjecture.

The record of the rounds count is #440.

items.title: The width of an induction
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

A new way back from the BWT introduced Cells, mibz2's experimental way of undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) that bzip2 applies to every block. Two posts this week cut the memory Cells uses: hand-me-down slots and one copy of each interval's details instead of two. This post asks a different question about the same memory: how much of it does the mathematics actually need at any one moment?

The recap. bzip2 sorts the rotations of a block and stores the last byte of each, the last column; each sorted rotation is a row. To decode, mibz2 follows a map called LF from row to row, reading one byte per step, which spells out the block backwards. A run is a stretch of equal bytes in the last column, and LF moves each run's rows as one shifted interval. Cells works on those intervals instead of on rows. Each step deletes some rows from the map and lets one interval jump straight over them. That interval now stands for more than one byte of text. When one interval is left, it stands for the whole block. The code calls each interval a letter, and the text it stands for its word. At the start there is one letter per run, and every word is one byte long.

What width is. At any moment of the rebuild, some letters still have a one-byte word. Each of those is an untouched piece of an original run. Its length, place and byte can be read off the list of runs, so in principle it needs no record of its own. Only the letters whose word has grown longer than one byte are new information. Call the most of those alive at once the width of the induction (the rebuild's sequence of steps), W. It is counted, like everything here, as a share of r, the number of runs in the block. Cells today writes a slot for every one of the r letters before its first step, and keeps r slots throughout.

What was found. Width depends on the order in which the steps are taken, by about three times.

  • Cells' order always takes its step at the right-hand end of the map. At its busiest it holds about 0.32 r letters with long words. That is the median over the 233 large blocks of the benchmark's Wikidata corpus, an extract of a Wikidata dump.
  • Taking the free steps first brings that peak down to about 0.08 to 0.12 r, depending on what is done when no free step is ready. It is 0.11 r if the rest follows Cells' own order. A free step is one whose bookkeeping creates no new boundary between intervals (section 3 shows one). The same order also takes about 20% fewer steps: 1.46 r instead of 1.84 r.
  • The free steps have a fixed end point. Taken in any order until none is left, they always reach the same state, in the same number of steps. That is now proved (#438). It follows that a kernel could take free steps in whichever order suits it, or share independent ones among threads. On Wikidata the end state has about 0.19 r letters, and no free-first order's peak exceeded it on any block.

How many letters the rebuild holds, per 100 runs of a Wikidata block

Letters, per 100 runs of the blockAt the start: one letter per run, each with a one-byte word100Cells writes a slot for every one before its first step.Peak with longer words: right end (Cells today)32Median of 233 Wikidata blocks; 27 to 36 per block.Letters left when the free steps run out19The same in any order (proved); on these blocks, no free-first peak exceeds it.Peak with longer words: free steps first, else right end11Median; 6 to 18 per block. Also 20% fewer steps: 1.46 r, not 1.84 r. Counted, not timed: medians over the 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows in the Wikidata corpus. Amber and green are the peaks of letters whose word is longer than one byte, under Cells’ right-end order and under free steps first. Grey is the number of letters, long words or not, left once the free steps run out.

What is classical and what is new. The steps are Rauzy–Veech induction, a 1979 construction in the theory of dynamical systems, and the words are the return words that theory has studied since. Counting the most words alive at once is not part of it. "Width" in this sense is not a standard term of that theory. It is a new measure, and its closest relatives are graph measures such as cutwidth: line a graph's vertices up, cut the line between any two, and count the edges that cross. Section 2 says where the line between old and new falls.

What this is not. These are counts, not timings. They come from one family of text, Wikidata's JSON, with four blocks of prose beside it. Prose gains less: the right end peaks at 0.37 r and free-first orders at 0.21 r. The link to cutwidth is a conjecture. Above all, no decoder that takes free steps first has been built or timed. Finding the free steps needs a worklist, which an earlier count priced at about 150 instructions a run against the right-end sweep's 115. Whether the smaller state pays for that is the next question, not an answer here.

Why mibz2 cares. Width is how much state the rebuild keeps in memory. When every thread decodes a block of its own, those states share the processor's cache, and the threads contend for it. Less state per block leaves less for the cache to hold. At ten threads on a 10-core Intel desktop, a block per thread takes 1.040 times the wall time of threads working in teams (95% interval 1.019 to 1.061; the run's report), so the margin is small. Lazy letters tested it: holding only the letters still in play, one block per thread beat the teams by 5% at ten threads, and mibz2 0.5.0 uses it from 8 threads up.

Section 1 works a nine-byte word by hand and draws its width. Section 2 says why only the long words count, and what is classical. Section 3 compares twelve orders of steps, and section 4 gives the bound and the theorem. Section 5 says what is open, and section 6 lists the reading.

items.title: The width of an induction: how much it must hold at once
items.text:
Taking the steps that cost no bookkeeping first would let mibz2 rebuild a block while keeping about a third as much in memory at its busiest moment.

15 November 2026 · 14 min read · Research in progress

items.title: 1. What does the rebuild hold, on a nine-byte word?
items.text:
Suppose you want to compress the word possesses. Its nine rotations, sorted, are its nine rows, and the last byte of each gives the last column sspssseeo. LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier in the text:

Row 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Last column s s p s s s e e o LF 4 5 3 6 7 8 0 1 2

The last column has five runs: ss, p, sss, ee and o. So the rebuild starts with five letters, each with a one-byte word.

Cells' order removes rows from the right-hand end, so the rows it still keeps are always a prefix, rows 0 to m − 1. Call m the cut. Each kept row's letter now jumps from that row along LF, through the removed rows, until it lands on a kept row again. Mathematicians call this the first return to the kept rows. The bytes read on the way, taken in text order, are the letter's word.

After four of its seven steps, Cells' order has cut the word at m = 4. The upper panel below draws that moment. Row 0, for example, reads s and goes to row 4. Row 4 is removed, so the path goes on, and reads s there. It goes on to row 7, also removed, and reads e. Then it returns to row 1, which is kept. Read in text order, its word is ess. Rows 1 and 3 likewise have the words oss and es. Row 2 goes straight to row 3, so its word is still the one byte p. Three letters out of four have long words, and that is the most this order ever holds on this word: its width is 3.

Under each kept row is its letter’s word: green where it is longer than one byte. Green arcs are the paths that build those words. The removed rows matter only as places a path passes through.

The lower panel takes the free steps first, and section 3 explains what makes a step free. It removes rows 0–2 first, not the right-hand end. It never holds more than two long words at once, so its width is 2. It also finishes in six steps, not seven. The counts after each step, from the start to the single letter at the end, are:

Each long word can be checked in possesses: ess, oss and es occur in it, and so do se and po. The steps themselves are animated, on the three-byte word aab, in the post that introduced Cells.

items.title: 2. Why do only the long words count?
items.text:
A letter whose word is one byte is a row, or a few adjacent rows, that LF sends straight to another kept row. It is a piece of an original run, cut shorter. Its first row, its length and the row it goes to all follow from the run it lies in. A decoder could leave it implicit and compute it when needed. A letter with a long word is different: where it jumps, and what it reads on the way, are the result of the steps taken so far.

The long words can be read from the arcs. A kept row has a long word exactly when its LF link crosses into the removed rows. Under Cells' order, the research record proves where each long-word letter begins (the census entry). It begins either at a run's first row whose link crosses the cut, or at the kept row whose path through the removed rows passes a run's first row. So the width counts crossings of the cut, bundled by runs.

Width, stated formally and read on possesses

1. First return. Let \(T\) be a bijection of a finite set \(X\) and \(D \subseteq X\). The first return of \(T\) to \(D\) is \(T_D(x) = T^{\tau(x)}(x)\), where \(\tau(x) \ge 1\) is the least power that lands back in \(D\).

Here \(T\) is LF on the rows \(\{0, \dots, n-1\}\), and \(D\) is the set of kept rows: \(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\) at the right end’s busiest moment.

2. Letters and words. \(T_D\) is a translation on each of finitely many intervals of \(D\). These are the letters \(\mathcal{A}_t\) after step \(t\). The word \(w_t(a)\) of a letter is the sequence of bytes read in its \(\tau\) moves, in text order, and \(|w_t(a)| = \tau\).

Here Row 0 takes \(\tau = 3\) moves, through rows 4 and 7, and reads ess. Row 2 takes one move, to row 3, and reads p.

3. Width. Over the steps of one order, \(W = \max_t \bigl|\{a \in \mathcal{A}_t : |w_t(a)| > 1\}\bigr|\). The number of steps is \(S\).

Here Right end: \(W = 3\), \(S = 7\). Free steps first: \(W = 2\), \(S = 6\). On Wikidata: \(W \approx 0.32\,r\) against \(0.11\,r\), and \(S \approx 1.84\,r\) against \(1.46\,r\).

Definitions 1 and 2 are the classical first-return construction behind Rauzy–Veech induction, for which Viana’s survey (2006) is an introduction, in a finite, discrete form: rows instead of a real interval. Definition 3 is the research record’s, not the literature’s.

What is classical. Inducing a map on a smaller set by its first return, and shrinking the set step by step, is Rauzy's induction (1979). Veech (1982) developed its dynamical and geometric meaning. Writing the orbit segments as words, so that each step becomes a substitution such as \(a \mapsto ab\), was made explicit by Lopez and Narbel (1999). Choosing a different path of steps, instead of always cutting at one end, is the branching Rauzy induction of Dolce and Perrin (2017).

What is new. That theory studies orbits, return times, invariant measures and coding. It does not ask how many words a computation must hold at once along a path of steps. Its usual setting also keeps the number of intervals fixed. In mibz2's discrete setting, a step between two letters of equal length deletes one, so the count falls as the rebuild goes on. The closest established ideas come from graph layout. Line up a graph's vertices in some order and cut the line after each prefix. The cutwidth of that order is the most edges any cut crosses, and vertex separation counts boundary vertices instead of edges. The least vertex separation over all orders equals the graph's pathwidth (Kinnersley 1992). Width here is the same kind of quantity, with the block's cycle of rows as the graph, its edges bundled into runs, and the kept rows as the prefix. Whether W is exactly a cutwidth is a conjecture. A stand-in for it, the runs crossing the cut upwards, peaks at 0.28 r over the 233 blocks. The exact count on 29 of them peaks at 0.31 r.

A trap in the terms. The geometric side of the theory draws each interval as a rectangle, in zippered rectangles, and calls the interval's length its rectangle's width. That is λ, a length, not a count of live words, and has nothing to do with W.

items.title: 3. Does the order of steps matter?
items.text:
Every step of the rebuild happens where a letter's interval in the map and another letter's landing place end on the same row. The research record calls such a row a coincidence. Cells' order always takes the coincidence at the right-hand end. Any other coincidence can be taken instead. Every order rebuilds the block, and the research record proves that the orders counted here build the same rules, the block's Lyndon tree (the Cells post's §5). They differ in when each rule is made, and so in how long each letter lives.

A step is free when it creates no new boundary: either the two letters have the same length, so one is deleted, or the shorter one's rows land where a boundary already is. In possesses at the start, the first free step is at the boundary after row 2. The letter on row 2, p, ends there, and so does the place where the letter on row 8, o, lands. Both are one row long. The step deletes row 2, and the letter on row 8 now jumps straight to row 3, where p went, reading po. A step that is not free, a paid step, splits an interval somewhere new, and a later step must remove that new boundary. Each free step removes one boundary and adds none.

The census ran twelve orders on every Wikidata block of at least 65,536 rows, and on the four prose blocks. Every final word was checked to be a rotation of its block (the orders entry; its summary). When no free step is ready, a free-first order needs a rule for the paid step: the right end, the largest cell, the smallest, or the leftmost. A cell is the stretch of rows a step removes. The orders "told from links" decide whether a step is free from the neighbouring letters alone, as a kernel would have to.

items.title: 4. How narrow can a free-first order be?
items.text:
Run free steps until none is left, and call the state reached the free closure. On Wikidata it leaves 0.185 r letters at the median (0.075 to 0.281 r), after 0.896 r steps.

The closure is the same whatever the order (proved). Free steps taken in any order until none is left always reach the same letters, the same words and the same number of steps. The one exception is a cycle of the map that closes completely within the free steps. Such a cycle takes no further part, and the orders can differ only in which rotation of its word it holds. No real block closes its cycle that early. The proof shows two things. Free steps always stop, since each removes a boundary. And any two free steps available together can be taken in either order and reach the same state again, which it checks case by case. By Newman's lemma, that is enough for a unique end point. A machine check of 10.7 million pairs of steps on short columns found no exception (#438, its entry and log). So the closure is a property of the block, like a normal form, and its size is a number the block determines.

The closure bounds the width (proved after it, counted before it). After the closure no step adds a letter, so the long words alive can never exceed the closure's letters again. Before the closure, the census found the same on every one of the 233 blocks, under three free-first orders. The width was at most 0.74 of the closure's letters, and 0.45 to 0.57 of them at the median. On a nine-byte word the bound can fail. Every step of beekeeper is free, so its closure is one letter, but its width under free steps first is at least 2. On real blocks the bound held without exception.

What follows for a kernel (a consequence, not a measurement). A kernel may take free steps in whichever order is cheapest for it, and still reach the same state. Free steps that touch different letters can be given to different threads, and they still reach that state. And a kernel that takes free steps first would need live state no larger than the closure, about 0.19 r letters. On these blocks its peak is nearer 0.11 r.

items.title: 5. What would it mean for mibz2?
items.text:
None of this is in the decoder. A kernel that used it would keep letters with one-byte words implicit, reading them from the run list, and write a letter only when its word first grows. Under Cells' order it would hold about 0.32 r letters at most; with free steps first, about 0.11 r. Cells today holds r.

The cost is in finding the steps. Cells sweeps the right-hand end, where the next step is always known, and that sweep is also why its cache misses are only first touches (#397). A free-first kernel needs a worklist of ready steps instead. An earlier count priced such a worklist at about 150 instructions a run against the sweep's 115, on one thread. Two things have changed in its favour since. The steps fall from 1.84 r to 1.47 r, and the state to hold falls by about three times. Whether that pays at ten threads sharing one last-level cache is a timing question, and it is the next one for the kernel work.

Three questions remain open:

  • Cutwidth. Is W exactly a cutwidth of the block's cycle, and can it be bounded from the run lengths alone? This is a conjecture.
  • Speed. Is any kernel that takes free steps first faster than Cells? Nothing has been timed.
  • The closure without the steps. An equal-length step says that every row of one letter goes next to the other: a forced adjacency. Genome assemblers join every forced adjacency at once when they compact a graph's unbranched paths, called unitigs. That compaction does not depend on any order. The conjecture is that the free closure is exactly that compaction. If so, it could be computed without simulating any step.

The width census and the order census are merged (#435, #437). The confluence proof, #438, is in review.

items.title: 6. Where to read more
items.text:
In order of use for this question:

  1. Marcelo Viana, Ergodic theory of interval exchange maps, Revista Matemática Complutense 19 (2006), 7–100. A survey, and the gentlest way in to first returns and Rauzy–Veech induction.
  2. Luis-Miguel Lopez and Philippe Narbel, Substitutions from Rauzy induction, in Developments in Language Theory (DLT 1999, World Scientific), 200–209. Rauzy induction read as substitutions on words.
  3. Francesco Dolce and Dominique Perrin, Interval exchanges, admissibility and branching Rauzy induction, RAIRO – Theoretical Informatics and Applications 51 (2017), 135–139 (arXiv). Choosing among many paths of steps, the freedom section 3 uses.
  4. Jon Fickenscher, Decoding Rauzy induction: an answer to Bufetov's general question, Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France 145 (2017), 603–621 (arXiv). Despite the title, not about decompression: it shows how an interval exchange is recovered from the products of its induction's steps.
  5. Gérard Rauzy, Échanges d'intervalles et transformations induites, Acta Arithmetica 34 (1979), 315–328, and William A. Veech, Gauss measures for transformations on the space of interval exchange maps, Annals of Mathematics 115 (1982), 201–242. The original papers; not the place to start for width.
  6. Josep Díaz, Jordi Petit and Maria Serna, A survey of graph layout problems, ACM Computing Surveys 34 (2002), 313–356. Cutwidth, vertex separation and their relatives.

items.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

One of mibz2's ways of rebuilding a block of bzip2 text works on fragments of it: pieces of the output, each standing for a stretch of the block. It keeps the bookkeeping for every fragment in a small record called a slot, 20 bytes holding the fragment's length, where its text is kept, the slot before it, and its partner slot in a second arrangement of the same fragments. When one fragment is finished, its slot is free just as the next fragment needs one, and mibz2 now hands it over instead of taking fresh memory.

items.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle: hand-me-down slots for every fragment of text
items.text:
Each new text fragment takes over the slot its finished neighbour just vacated, so mibz2 touches 30% fewer slots and needs up to 15% less memory.

15 November 2026 · 13 min read · Research result

items.title: The idea in a nutshell
items.text:
Slot recycling makes mibz2 faster by recognising that, whenever its Cells algorithm needs somewhere to put a new piece of information, another piece of information has just finished using its space.

Previously, the algorithm reserved a fresh memory slot for the new piece, leaving the old slot behind. Now, it reuses the old slot immediately.

This is a deceptively simple improvement. The algorithm still performs the same mathematical operations and reconstructs exactly the same bytes. What changes is how much memory it needs to touch while doing so.

On the Wikidata benchmark, slot recycling:

  • Eliminates 29.7% of the slots previously touched during Cells induction.
  • Reduces peak decoder memory usage by 10–15%.
  • Makes four-thread decoding 1.7% faster in the initial paired CI benchmark, without a statistically established speed change at one or two threads.

The important insight is that we aren't making the mathematics smaller; we're making its physical representation more efficient. We're taking advantage of something already guaranteed by the mathematics: one slot's useful lifetime ends just as another begins.

And because mibz2's performance is sensitive to memory contention, eliminating unnecessary memory accesses can matter more than shaving a few arithmetic instructions.

items.title: 1. Why memory matters so much to mibz2
items.text:
To understand why this is worthwhile, we need to understand what mibz2 spends much of its time doing.

Bzip2 compression uses the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which rearranges a block's bytes into an order that's easier to compress. Decompression must reverse that rearrangement and recover the original text.

The conventional way to reverse the BWT is to construct a permutation describing where each position leads, then follow that permutation to reconstruct the original sequence.

This is computationally awkward for modern processors.

Each step tells the processor where to look next. The address of the following memory access often cannot be known until the current access completes. If the relevant data isn't in cache, the processor may spend much of its time waiting for memory.

mibz2's original approach was to interleave several independent traversals, allowing the processor to have multiple memory operations in flight.

But the Cells algorithm takes a more radical approach.

Instead of reconstructing the text by following the permutation one position at a time, Cells exploits the structure of the permutation itself.

The inverse-BWT permutation has a special organisation: it acts as a translation over intervals corresponding to runs of equal bytes. That allows it to be treated as a finite interval-exchange system.

Using a form of Rauzy–Veech induction, Cells repeatedly simplifies this system. Each simplification combines pieces of the permutation and builds a compact description of the text they represent.

Eventually, the algorithm has enough information to reconstruct the original block.

This can require dramatically fewer algorithmic steps than following every position in the original permutation.

However, those steps have their own cost: Cells must maintain a changing representation of the intervals, their relationships and the words they represent.

That representation is where slot recycling operates.

items.title: 2. What is a slot?
items.text:
Imagine that Cells is manipulating a collection of pieces, which we'll call letters. Each letter represents an interval together with a word: the sequence of output bytes associated with it.

The induction maintains two orderings of these letters, corresponding to the two sides of the interval exchange.

We can think of them as:

  • The top order, describing one arrangement of the pieces.
  • The bottom order, describing the corresponding arrangement on the other side.

These aren't two complete copies of the decompressed text. They're two linked arrangements of the same mathematical pieces.

Each letter has a slot in each order.

Here are both orders for a handful of letters, with each letter's two slots joined:

Two linked orders of the same letters

Top orderA is at its frontBottom orderB is at its frontfront: read firstfront: read first…DCBA…CADBeach slot links to the slot before it in its orderpartner: the same letter’s slot in the other order Conceptual: five slots of each order. Each letter has a slot in both orders, in a different arrangement, so the partner links cross. The induction reads each order from its front, where A and B are, and follows the links to the slots before them.

A slot is a small record in memory. In the implementation shipped before this change, it occupies 20 bytes, containing the information needed to navigate and manipulate the induction:

Information Purpose Previous-slot link Finds the next piece when advancing through the order Interval length Describes how many positions the piece covers Word reference and length Identifies the text represented by the piece Partner-slot reference Connects its position in one order to the corresponding position in the other

The slot's five fields, as the code lays them out:

A slot is 20 bytes: five 4-byte fields

048121620byteslot before4 B · link in its orderletter’s length4 B · positions leftword’s length4 B · in bytesword’s offset4 B · bytes or a rulepartner slot4 B · in the other orderthe word: read as one 8-byte load20 bytes, five 4-byte fieldsA 64-byte cache lineholds 3.2 slots, so slots straddle linesslot 1slot 2slot 364 bytesnext The layout as src/cells.rs documents it, unchanged by #408. Every field is a 4-byte offset or length. The table above lists the word’s length and offset as one row, since the induction reads them together. Below, to scale: 64 bytes hold three whole slots and part of a fourth.

The algorithm walks through these two orders, repeatedly taking pieces from their fronts.

As it goes, it transforms letters into cells: finished pieces whose words can be represented by literal bytes or by references to previously constructed words.

The slot records are the bookkeeping that makes this transformation possible.

And because there can be many millions of cells, even seemingly small inefficiencies in this bookkeeping accumulate.

items.title: 3. How an induction step works
items.text:
At each step, Cells considers two pieces, A and B, one encountered through each order.

Suppose their remaining interval lengths are:

  • A has length 7.
  • B has length 3.

The algorithm takes the smaller length, 3, and constructs a cell representing the corresponding portions of A and B. Its word is constructed by concatenating their associated words.

Now B has been exhausted, while A still has 4 positions remaining.

Conceptually:

One unequal step: B ends, A goes on

Before the stepA7B3the cell: min(7, 3) = 3at the front of bothone stepAfter the stepAgoes on, with 4 leftBhas endedcelllength 3word: A’s word, then B’s Conceptual: the example in the text. Each square is one position. The green squares become the cell; A’s other four stay A’s. B ends, so its slot in the bottom order is free from this step on.

This is a simplification of the mathematical operation, but it captures the essential event.

One letter continues. The other finishes.

If A and B had equal remaining lengths, both would finish together. The interesting case for slot recycling is when their lengths differ, because the surviving letter will eventually produce another cell.

That next cell needs a place in the other ordering.

Previously, the algorithm reserved a fresh slot for it.

But notice what has just happened: the other letter, B, has finished. Its position at the front of that ordering is no longer needed.

This is where the opportunity appears.

items.title: 4. The old approach: make room for a future cell
items.text:
The original implementation was designed to avoid complicated rearrangements of the linked orders.

When a letter continued after an unequal-length step, Cells promised it a slot for its next cell. That slot came from additional space reserved beyond the original letters' slots.

This was straightforward and efficient in an important sense: it avoided having to move existing letters or reorganise the whole structure.

But every promise of a fresh slot extended the set of memory locations the induction would eventually touch.

Across millions of steps, many of these fresh locations occupied cache lines that had not previously been used.

Touching a new cache line may require the processor to bring it into cache, obtain write ownership and eventually evict or write back dirty data. These costs become particularly significant when several workers are competing for limited cache capacity.

Meanwhile, some original slots were already dead.

The algorithm had information about their former contents in registers, yet their memory locations were being left unused.

We had space becoming available at precisely the moment we were reserving more space elsewhere.

items.title: 5. The new approach: recycle the slot that just died
items.text:
Slot recycling changes how that promised location is chosen.

Returning to our example, B has just finished and A continues.

Previously, the next cell cut from A would receive a fresh slot in the bottom order.

Now it receives B's former front slot in that same order.

Here is the bottom order after B ends, before and after the change:

The bottom order after B ends: where A’s next cell goes

Before #408: a fresh slot past the letters…DAnow the cellCBdead, leftthe frontjust readend of the letters’ slotsA’s nextfresh slotroom for one freshslot per cellA’s next cell is promised a slot never touched beforeWith #408: the dead front slot is recycled…DAnow the cellCA’s nextwas B’sthe frontjust readend of the letters’ slotspromised B’s old slotno slot past herethe region is letters × 20 B Conceptual, after the step in the last figure. Slots are in memory order; the front is the slot the induction reads next, and it moves left as the induction goes on. The promised slot is linked in as the slot before A’s cell, so A’s next cell will be read there. The cell is also written to B’s slot in the top order (not drawn). When A ends instead, the same happens in the top order, with A’s front slot.

This isn't an ordinary memory allocator discovering that a block of memory happens to be free. The algorithm knows, from the structure of its induction, that this specific slot has become available.

The implementation has three crucial facts in its favour.

First, the finished letter cannot be encountered again through that old front slot. It was the last remaining piece at the front of its order, and no surviving link leads back to the slot as that letter.

Second, its corresponding position in the other order has already been replaced by the newly constructed cell. The pairing and links have been updated to refer to the new structure.

Third, everything the current operation still needs from the finished letter has already been read into registers. The old slot's memory contents are no longer required.

Together, these facts establish that the slot can safely take on a new purpose.

Instead of advancing a cursor into fresh storage, the algorithm remembers the location of the slot it just consumed.

In the Rust implementation, two offsets, fa and fb, track the front slots in the respective orders. When one letter finishes and the other continues, the appropriate front offset becomes the promised location.

The surrounding induction remains essentially unchanged. It creates the same cells, constructs the same words and ultimately produces the same decompressed output.

The difference is that its slots are reused rather than continually extended.

That is why the name slot recycling is so precise.

items.title: 6. How much does this save?
items.text:
The builder, the agent that implemented #408, counted what happened across the 196 Wikidata blocks admitted by Cells in the benchmark corpus.

The result was substantial:

Quantity Before After Slots touched 31,547,362 22,181,734 Fresh slots required 9,365,628 0 Reduction in touched slots — 29.7%

The same counts, drawn to scale:

Slots the induction touches, over the 196 Wikidata blocks

Beforeletters’ slots 22,181,734fresh 9,365,62831,547,362Afterletters’ slots 22,181,734−29.7%, no fresh slot9,365,628 slots × 20 B = 187.3 MB no longer touched, 0.89 B per output byte, over the 196 blocks Counted, not timed: #408’s census of the benchmark’s Wikidata corpus, the 196 of its 431 blocks that Cells admits. The letters’ slots are two per letter, one in each order. Every unequal cell used to take one fresh slot.

Each avoided slot is 20 bytes.

Across those blocks, this corresponds to approximately 187 million bytes of slot storage no longer touched.

That doesn't mean precisely 187 million fewer bytes travel to DRAM. Cache lines, write allocation, reuse and eviction behaviour determine actual memory traffic.

But it does mean that millions of distinct slot locations are no longer needed.

The allocation can shrink too. The previous implementation reserved room for additional slots based on its cell budget. The new one needs only enough room for the original letters' slots in each order.

And this matters beyond the amount of memory allocated.

items.title: Why fewer slots can mean faster decoding
items.text:
Modern CPUs don't fetch arbitrary individual bytes directly from main memory for ordinary cached accesses. They work with cache lines, commonly 64 bytes.

A 20-byte slot is small, but enough slots spread over millions of addresses occupy a substantial working set.

When several workers decode different blocks simultaneously, each has its own induction state competing for space in the shared cache.

If their combined working sets are too large, useful data gets displaced, and later accesses may have to retrieve it from slower levels of the memory hierarchy.

Slot recycling attacks that problem directly.

The slot being recycled has only just been read, so its cache line may already be resident. The fresh location it replaces might otherwise require a first touch of a different line.

The immediate benefit isn't fewer mathematical operations. It's less memory to keep resident and fewer distinct places to access.

This explains why the change is especially interesting for parallel decoding.

items.title: 7. What the benchmarks tell us
items.text:
The initial paired CI benchmark measured the complete decoder, rather than just timing the induction function in isolation.

For Wikidata:

Threads Wall-time change Peak memory change 1 +0.5% −9.7% 2 −0.2% −12.5% 4 −1.7% −14.6%

The same run with its intervals, and the memory in megabytes:

The decoder on Wikidata, with and without slot recycling

Wall time, head against basePeak memory, base → head1 thread+0.5%1 thread33 MB30 MB, −9.7%2 threads−0.2%2 threads71 MB62 MB, −12.5%4 threads−1.7%4 threads109 MB96 MB, −14.6%−4%−3%−2%−1%0%+1%+2%← faster · slower →basehead, with #408 Measured: #408’s paired CI bench, 10 rounds on one runner (Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, 4 CPUs on 2 cores), the whole decoder on the Wikidata corpus. Left: the change in median wall time with its 95% interval across the rounds; green where the interval excludes no change. Right: peak resident memory, each a reduction the bench reports as beyond noise. The records corpus was 3.4% slower at 4 threads in the same run.

The four-thread wall-time improvement had a reported 95% confidence interval of −3.3% to −0.1%.

That is a modest but positive result on this runner. The one- and two-thread changes were indistinguishable from noise.

The memory reductions are much larger.

This pattern is consistent with the intended mechanism: reducing the working set matters more as concurrency increases.

But we should be precise about what has been established. The CI runner isn't the i9 workstation. It has a different cache hierarchy and different core-sharing conditions. The benchmark demonstrates a benefit on the tested machine, but it doesn't yet establish how much slot recycling helps the i9's known concurrency plateau.

A later paired run on the i9, a 10-core desktop, shows the gain growing with the number of Cells workers: no change at one or two threads, 4% less CPU at four, and 5% faster wall time at five (interval 4.7% to 6.1%). Peak memory was lower at every thread count from one to five, and nothing changed at six or more threads, where mibz2 uses its team path instead of Cells.

There's also a secondary-workload caveat: the records corpus showed a four-thread regression in the same CI run. Correctness was preserved, but the change is not a universal speedup.

The valuable thing is that the memory reduction is substantial without requiring additional expensive computation. The extra bookkeeping is minimal, with the front positions already available to the induction.

items.title: 8. Why this is different from field elision
items.text:
The terminology initially caused some confusion because two related research ideas both used the word elision.

MONODROMY, the team's mathematics agent, investigated whether individual fields inside existing slots could be left unwritten or reconstructed from other information.

It found that approximately 25.5% of the induction's stored bytes were never subsequently read, and that certain mathematical identities could account for an even larger fraction.

That sounds promising, but almost every redundant field shares its 64-byte cache line with live information.

If you stop writing a redundant field while leaving the surrounding record layout unchanged, the processor may still need the same cache line.

So removing those field writes doesn't necessarily make the working set smaller.

Slot recycling solves a different problem.

It doesn't selectively remove fields from slots. It removes the need for whole additional slots.

That means entire ranges of memory no longer need to be touched, and the required working set can genuinely shrink.

This distinction is central:

  • Field elision: store less information in the same locations.
  • Slot recycling: use fewer locations to store the necessary information.
  • Equal-cell elision: avoid constructing some cells altogether, replacing those operations with another reconstruction mechanism.

The third idea remains a separate mathematical opportunity. Slot recycling hasn't implemented it or disproved it.

items.title: 9. Why the change is safe
items.text:
Reusing memory in an algorithm implemented with unchecked offsets and unsafe Rust deserves particular care.

The crucial correctness obligation is not merely that a slot looks unused. It must be guaranteed that no later operation still needs its old contents.

The proof comes from the induction's ordering invariant: the consumed front slot has no surviving references as the old letter, and its necessary values have already been captured.

The implementation also narrows the slot regions to the exact number of original letters. Tests check that promised slots stay inside those regions, including cases where there is no spare room beyond them.

The builder compared the new induction against the original on exhaustive small inputs, accounting for the fact that physical slot offsets legitimately differ. The resulting words, rules, state and output agree.

The broader decoder tests, CRC checks and Miri validation passed before the change was merged.

This is important because the optimisation changes where state lives, not what that state means.

The resulting decoder remains subject to the same correctness requirements as before.

items.title: 10. What this teaches us about improving mibz2
items.text:
Slot recycling is a good example of why sophisticated algorithms still benefit from careful attention to mundane-looking implementation details.

The Cells algorithm is built on substantial mathematics: interval exchanges, Rauzy–Veech induction, permutation structure and compact representations of words.

That mathematics makes it possible to avoid much of the work required by conventional inverse-BWT traversal.

But the mathematical abstraction also introduces a physical representation: linked orders, slots, words and rules.

The performance of the resulting program depends on both levels.

An algorithm can have excellent asymptotic properties and still spend too much time managing its intermediate state.

Conversely, improving that state management can produce worthwhile gains without changing the underlying algorithm at all.

The particularly elegant aspect of slot recycling is that it derives the optimisation from a structural property of Cells itself.

At every unequal induction step, the continued letter needs a future slot just as the exhausted letter releases one.

Recognising that relationship removes a whole category of unnecessary memory use.

The successful change therefore sits at the intersection of mathematics and systems programming: a proof about object lifetimes becomes a more efficient memory layout, which becomes a measurable improvement in the complete decoder.

It also points towards the next questions.

MONODROMY has identified a possible asymmetric layout with 20-byte top slots and 8-byte bottom slots. That could mean up to 25% fewer induction lines (an estimate made before recycling), although it introduces an additional dependent load on many accesses. It remains unmeasured, and the earlier failed 16-byte layout is a warning that compactness isn't automatically speed.

Meanwhile, measuring how memory traffic scales after slot recycling can help determine whether Cells is becoming competitive at higher thread counts.

Those are separate experiments. Slot recycling has already justified itself on its own evidence.

items.title: The essential insight
items.text:
Slot recycling makes mibz2 better by exploiting the fact that the useful lifetime of one memory record ends exactly when another needs its space.

It doesn't eliminate the induction steps. It doesn't change the text reconstruction. It doesn't require a more elaborate parallel algorithm.

It simply stops the program from touching memory it never needed to touch.

That's why a change that is small in code can remove nearly a third of the induction's touched slots — and why understanding the mathematical structure of an algorithm can yield practical improvements well beyond the mathematics itself.

Implementation and evidence: mibz2 PR #408, merged on 15 November. For the distinction between slot recycling and field elision, see MONODROMY's analysis, PR #410.

items.title: Lazy letters
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

The width of an induction counted how much of a block's rebuild must be held in memory at once, and found it was about a third of what mibz2's Cells kernel actually lays out. This post is about a kernel that keeps only that third, called lazy letters, and about what happened when ten threads ran it at once on a 10-core machine.

On a 10-core Intel i9, with each thread decoding a block of its own, lazy letters cut the wall time against mibz2 0.4.0 by 4.2% at 8 threads, 10.8% at 9 and 5.1% at 10. At 10 threads mibz2 0.4.0 runs teams of threads that share a block, so there lazy letters make one block per thread beat the teams. At 4 and 6 threads the extra instructions outweigh the saving, and lazy letters are 3% to 9% slower.

The recap. bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900 kB. Each block goes through the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), which reorders its bytes so that equal bytes sit together in runs. Undoing it means following a map from row to row of the sorted block. Cells, mibz2's kernel for most blocks of the benchmark's Wikidata text, does that on intervals instead of rows. It starts with one interval per run. Each step of the rebuild (the induction) shortens the map by letting one interval stand for a longer piece of text. The code calls each interval a letter and the text it stands for its word. When one letter is left, its word is the whole block. Cells keeps each letter's bookkeeping (its length, where its word is, its neighbours) in a record called a slot.

What width is. A letter whose word is still one byte long is an untouched piece of an original run: everything about it can be read off the list of runs. Only the letters the rebuild has already changed hold new information. The most of those alive at any one moment is the width. On Wikidata it is about 0.32 of the letters, under the order of steps Cells takes. Cells today lays out a slot for every letter before its first step, and keeps them all until the end.

Why mibz2 cares. Width is how much state the rebuild keeps in memory. When every thread decodes a block of its own, those states share the processor's cache, and the threads contend for it. Keeping less live state per block eases that.

items.title: Lazy letters: just-in-time memory for induction
items.text:
Holding fewer letters at once leaves the cache less crowded, so eight to ten threads decode up to 11% faster despite extra instructions.

16 November 2026 · 11 min read · Research result

items.title: What was found
items.text:
The takeaways, each shown in a section below:

  • Lazy letters keep a third of the slots. An interval the rebuild hasn't reached yet is kept as a 5-byte entry, and gets a slot only when a step first reaches it. Slots that are finished with go back to a pool. The pool's peak matches the width, 0.318 of the letters, to three digits. The memory the rebuild touches besides its output falls by 38% (section 1).
  • It costs instructions. The first stage and the induction together take 28% more instructions. Every letter is now visited twice, and the inner loop runs short of registers (section 2).
  • At 4 and 6 threads it loses; from 8 it wins. On a 10-core Intel i9, lazy letters take 3% to 9% more wall time than mibz2 0.4.0 at 4 and 6 threads. From 8 to 10 threads they take 4% to 11% less (section 3).
  • At 10 threads it beats the teams. From ten threads, mibz2 doesn't give each thread a block of its own. It runs teams of threads that share a block, because one block per thread was slower there. Lazy letters reverse that: one block per thread is 5.1% faster than the teams, at 10.6% more processor time.
  • The gain grows with the thread count, as contention for the cache predicts. Against the current kernel, lazy letters fare better at 10 threads than at 4 in all ten paired rounds (section 4).
  • Since 0.5.0 it is the default from 8 threads. This is one machine and one text. mibz2 0.5.0 uses lazy letters whenever each thread decodes a block of its own at 8 threads or more, and a confirming run on the i9 is queued (section 5).

How much faster mibz2 decodes with lazy letters, by thread count

◀ slowerfaster ▶-10%-5%0+5%+10%+15%wall time saved, as a percentage (bar: 95% interval)4 threadsvs mibz2 now: a block per thread4 threads: 8.6% slower (95% interval -10.2% to -7.0%)8.6% slower6 threadsvs mibz2 now: a block per thread6 threads: 3.3% slower (95% interval -4.8% to -1.9%)3.3% slower8 threadsvs mibz2 now: a block per thread8 threads: 4.2% faster (95% interval +2.0% to +6.4%)4.2% faster9 threadsvs mibz2 now: a block per thread9 threads: 10.8% faster (95% interval +9.1% to +12.5%)10.8% faster10 threadsvs mibz2 now: teams of threads10 threads: 5.1% faster (95% interval +3.4% to +6.7%)5.1% faster12 threadsvs mibz2 now: teams of threads12 threads: 1.8% slower (95% interval -5.1% to +1.4%)no change detected Lazy letters, one block per thread, against mibz2 0.4.0 on an Intel i9-10900K with 10 cores, decoding an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump, 10 paired rounds per thread count. Below 10 threads mibz2 already gives each thread a block of its own, so only the kernel differs. From 10 threads it runs teams of threads that share a block, so at 10 threads lazy letters makes one block per thread beat the teams. 12 threads uses the cores’ second hardware threads; its interval spans zero. The crossover between 6 and 8 threads is why the production version switches to lazy letters only from 8 threads up.

items.title: 1. What does a block keep while it is rebuilt?
items.text:
Cells tracks the letters in two orders. The first is the order of the runs in the block. The second is the same runs sorted by byte value, keeping runs with the same byte in their original order. Each step works at the right-hand end of both orders, at what the code calls the two fronts. It compares the two letters there, records a cell (one piece of a word, added to a list of rules the writer later expands into text), and moves on. The fronts work backwards from the end, so at any moment most letters are still ahead of them, untouched.

Cells in 0.4.0 gives every letter a slot before the first step. A slot is 20 bytes in the kernel's own buffer, holding the letter's length, its links and where its word is. A second slot, 8 bytes in the output buffer, holds its links in the other order. (The output buffer is free to use until the writer runs, at the very end.) Most of those slots sit unused for most of the rebuild, because most letters are still untouched pieces of runs.

Lazy letters keep an untouched letter as 5 bytes in the output buffer instead. A 4-byte entry in the second order holds its length, its byte and whether the decoder's walk starts there. One more byte, in the first order, repeats its byte. That is all a step needs until a front first reaches the letter. The step itself is unchanged: the same cells, in the same order, written as the same words at the same places.

How lazy letters keep a letter, from untouched to finished

An untouched letter, in the output bufferentry, 4 byteslength · byte · whether the walk starts herein the second order (sorted by byte)1 byteits bytein the first order5 BA letter’s three statesUntouchedthe 5-byte entry aboveuntil a front first reaches itIn playa pair of slots from the poolsits entry now points to the pairFinishedthe pair goes on the free listthe next letter reached reuses ita freed pair is handed to the next letter a front reaches (last in, first out) Conceptual. A letter costs 5 bytes until a front reaches it, then holds a pair of slots while it is in play. When it is finished (merged away at a step between two letters of equal length, or closed), its pair goes back on a last-in-first-out free list for the next letter a front reaches.

Two facts, both in the research journal, mean nothing else needs storing. First, within one byte value, the two orders list the letters in the same order. So a counter for each of the 256 byte values finds a letter's entry in the second order from its byte, with no stored map between the orders (which would cost another 4 bytes a letter). Second, a front reaches a letter first from one order only, and never reads that entry again. So the entry, once used, is overwritten with a tagged pointer to the letter's new slots, for the other front to follow when it gets there.

What the rebuild keeps, eager and lazy

Ten intervals of a block, part-way through the rebuildEager (Cells in 0.4.0)a slot for every interval, laid out before the first stepaslotbslotcslotdsloteslotfslotgslothslotislotjslotLazy lettersan untouched interval is a 5-byte entry; a slot is taken when the rebuild reaches itagiven backb5 Bcslotd5 Be5 Bfslotg5 Bhsloti5 Bj5 BBytes per letter that the rebuild touches, besides the outputEagerslots: 20 B per letterslots 20words: 15.6 B per letterwords 15.635.6 BLazy letterspool: 6.4 B per letterpool 6.4words: 15.6 B per letterwords 15.622.0 BThe words (arena and rules, 15.6 B) are the same in both. In the output buffer, eager keeps 8 B a letter;lazy letters keep the 5-byte entry and 2.5 B of a second pool. Bars start at zero. Above: conceptual, ten letters at one moment. Below: counted on one thread over the 196 Wikidata blocks Cells handles (11,090,867 letters), per letter, besides the output buffer. The lazy pool's bytes follow from its peak, the median over blocks.

The count. Over Wikidata's 196 blocks, the pool peaks at a median of 0.318 of the letters. No block goes above 0.337. That equals the width the earlier post counted for Cells' right-end order, 0.318, to three digits: the pool holds a pair for each letter the fronts have reached that is still alive. So the memory the kernel holds now follows the width, not the letter count. Per letter:

Bytes per letter, Wikidata 0.4.0 Lazy letters Slots in the kernel's buffer 20.0 6.4 Words (the rules and their store) 15.6 15.6 Total besides the output 35.6 22.0 Inside the output buffer, before the writer 8.0 7.5

The 6.4 bytes are the 20-byte slots of the letters in play at the peak: about 20 × 0.318. Inside the output buffer, lazy letters keep the 5-byte entries. They also keep second-order slots for the letters in play, about 8 × 0.318, or 2.5 bytes a letter. The pools have room for a slot for every letter, so the memory set aside is not smaller; what falls is the memory handed out and touched. Every block decodes to the same bytes as before.

items.title: 2. What does keeping less cost?
items.text:
The same count says what it costs. Per letter, on one thread:

Instructions per letter 0.4.0 Lazy letters First stage (laying out the letters) 81.0 71.2 Induction 115.5 181.0 Both together 196.4 252.2 (+28%)

The first stage gets cheaper, since it writes 5 bytes a letter instead of a slot. The induction gets much dearer, for two reasons. Every letter is now visited twice as each order is read, once untouched and once after it has a slot, and each visit tests which it is. The shipped kernel reads a slot each time with no test. And the lazy loop holds about 30 values at once, against the shipped loop's 19. That is more than the processor has registers for, so some spill to the stack and are reloaded.

These are instruction counts, not times. A first build cost 36% more; a leaner one, which takes slots only in the branches that need them, brought that to 28%. Before any timing, the kernel was set a limit of 10% more instructions, and at +28% it failed it. It was kept as a recorded result, with the open question of whether 38% less memory would outweigh the instructions with ten threads sharing one cache. Only a clock on a 10-core machine could answer that.

items.title: 3. What happened on ten cores?
items.text:
The machine is the maintainer's workstation, an Intel i9-10900K. It has 10 cores, each with two hardware threads, and they all share one 20 MiB last-level cache. The run decoded the Wikidata extract at six thread counts from 4 to 12, in 10 paired rounds each. It compared four arms. The first is mibz2 0.4.0. The second gives each thread a block, with the current kernel, and the third does the same with lazy letters. The fourth is described below. All 240 readings produced the same output.

The rule, set before the data. The decision rule compared lazy letters with one block per thread on the current kernel, so that only the kernel differed. Memory would count as the cause if lazy letters were faster at 10 threads, with the interval wholly below 1, and level or slower at 4. As a sanity check, the plain one-block-per-thread arm had to match mibz2 0.4.0 at 4 to 9 threads, where they run the same plan. It did: every one of those four intervals spans 1.

The outcome. Lazy letters were 8.4% slower at 4 threads, as their extra instructions predict. At 10 threads they were 8.1% faster, with an interval of 6.5% to 9.8%. The rule's case is met. Against mibz2 0.4.0, which is what a user ran then, the figures by thread count are:

Threads 4 6 8 9 10 12 Wall time, lazy ÷ 0.4.0 1.086 1.033 0.958 0.892 0.949 1.018 95% interval 1.070–1.102 1.019–1.048 0.936–0.980 0.875–0.909 0.933–0.966 0.986–1.051 Processor time, lazy ÷ 0.4.0 1.106 1.059 0.959 0.885 1.106 1.546 What mibz2 0.4.0 runs a block per thread a block per thread a block per thread a block per thread 3 teams of 3 3 teams of 3

At 8 and 9 threads lazy letters are faster and use less processor time as well. At 10 the comparison is with the teams. Teams were chosen there because, on this machine, one block per thread had been 4% slower than the teams at ten threads (the earlier run). With lazy letters, one block per thread is 5.1% faster than the teams instead, at 10.6% more processor time. At 12 threads, two threads share some cores. No change in wall time was detected there, and processor time rose by 55%.

Memory, measured as the whole process's peak. One block per thread holds ten blocks' state at once, and teams hold only three. At 10 threads the teams peaked at 73 MB. One block per thread peaked at 191 MB with the current kernel and 186 MB with lazy letters. Lazy letters cut the rebuild's working memory, but a plan that decodes ten blocks at once still uses far more memory than one that decodes three.

The fourth arm: rules written past the cache. The induction writes each new word's description, a rule, and never reads it back; the writer reads the rules afterwards. Writing them with non-temporal stores, which bypass the cache, saves cache space without changing the amount of memory. At 10 threads no difference was detected (1.011, interval 0.985 to 1.037). At 4 threads it was 2.6% slower. That idea stays closed.

items.title: 4. Why would fewer bytes help only with many threads?
items.text:
On one thread, the cache holds a block's working state comfortably, and the processor's time goes on instructions. That is why lazy letters lose at 4 threads: they do more work, and the memory they save was not in short supply.

With a block per thread, each thread's state competes for the one shared cache. A rough calculation shows the scale. A Wikidata block that Cells handles has about 56,600 letters on average. At 35.6 bytes a letter, the rebuild touches about 2.0 MB besides its output. Ten threads together touch about 20 MB, the size of the i9's whole last-level cache. At 22.0 bytes a letter, it is about 1.2 MB a block and 12 MB for ten. This is arithmetic on averages, not a measurement of the cache. The output buffers and the decoder's other stages also use the cache, and not all of a block's state is in use at the same moment.

The measurement that supports contention is the pattern across thread counts. If the extra instructions were the only effect, lazy letters' ratio against the current kernel would be about the same at every count. Instead it falls as threads are added, from 1.084 at 4 threads to 0.919 at 10. The rule asked whether the 10-thread ratio was below the 4-thread ratio round by round. It was in all ten paired rounds (sign test, p = 0.002). At 12 threads, where hardware threads share cores, the ratio against the current kernel falls further, to 0.852. Cache misses were not counted in this run. So this is evidence from timing that memory per core costs time at high thread counts, not a direct observation of the cache. It doesn't say which part of the memory system is the limit: the cache's capacity, the misses themselves, or the bandwidth to main memory. Hardware counters, or runs designed to separate them, would.

items.title: 5. What comes next?
items.text:
Accepting the processor time. At 10 threads, lazy letters use 10.6% more processor time than the teams. mibz2's release rules send any rise over 10% to the maintainer, and he accepted it. The extra processor time mattered only as a sign of contention for the cache, and the wall time fell.

In 0.5.0. mibz2 0.5.0 uses lazy letters for one block per thread from 8 threads up, and the current kernel below, chosen by one constant in the decoder's thread plan. The old kernel stays selectable, so the two can be compared at the same commit. A run at the release, on the i9 from 4 to 20 threads, confirms the switch point under a rule fixed before it. It also decides whether one block per thread should replace the teams at more thread counts. A move into counts above the 10 cores, where threads share a core, goes back to the maintainer with the figures.

A better order of steps. Lazy letters still take Cells' order, always at the right-hand end, and the pool's peak is that order's width. Other orders build the same rules while finishing letters sooner. The order census found that taking the steps that need no new bookkeeping first, the free steps, brings the median width on Wikidata from 0.318 to 0.107 of the runs. Newer simulations, in review, choose each step by how much it changes the width. One that still prefers free steps peaks at 0.077 of the runs, and one that puts the change in width first at 0.058. These are counts from a simulator, not a kernel. They also have a cost the counts leave out: lazy letters read the untouched letters as two streams from the right-hand end, and any other order needs letters that neither front has reached yet. Priced against the kernel's own bytes, that cost decides it for now. The slots are under a third of what lazy letters touch, and the index any other order needs adds about 8 bytes a letter, so no order cut the kernel's bytes by the quarter the rule asked. Orders that read only near the two streams, which would need no index, are still being counted. The same run will also measure how much slower a block is at 10 threads than at 1, for each kernel, which says how much of the high-thread penalty memory still accounts for.

What changes in how memory cuts are judged. Lazy letters failed their own instruction limit and still won where it matters for many threads. Earlier memory cuts were rejected because they cost instructions at 1 to 4 threads. From now on a memory cut is judged by its peak live memory per block and by wall time at 8 to 10 threads.

Since 0.5.0, lazy letters are the default kernel for one block per thread from 8 threads up.

The chain, in short, runs like this. The rebuild needs only a third of the slots Cells lays out. A kernel that keeps only those cuts the working memory by 38%, at 28% more instructions. With few threads that is a loss. With ten threads sharing one cache it is a gain, enough for a block per thread to beat the teams. When threads share a cache, the bytes a block keeps can matter more than the instructions it runs.

Research records:

  • The kernel's design and counts: 2026-11-15-lazy-letters.md.
  • The experiment's arms, safety arguments and recipe: 2026-11-15-memory-lever.md and its counts (#447).
  • The decision rule, set before the run: the team channel, 15 November.
  • The run's verdict: the team channel, 15 November. Its results bundle: run-20261115T233002Z.tar.gz, with summary.txt (against mibz2 0.4.0), summary-workers.txt (against one block per thread) and lever.txt (round by round).
  • The production plan and the follow-ups: the team channel, 15 November and again.
  • Background: the width of an induction and the free closure of an induction.

items.title: A mathematical dictionary
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2, our bzip2 decoder, inverts each block's Burrows–Wheeler transform with a kernel we call Cells. Over the past week our notes have described it in a working vocabulary of letters, words, cells, rules, steps, a marked row, a writer and a stop. They have also borrowed three pictures from Robert Ghrist's Elementary Applied Topology: discrete Morse theory, sheaves of monoids, and circular coordinates. This post says exactly which mathematical object each of our words names, and how far each borrowed picture holds.

The setting, in brief. bzip2 stores a block as the last column \(L\) of its sorted rotations, the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), together with the row that holds the original text. A map called LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. Following LF from that row reads the block backwards, one byte per step. A run is a stretch of equal bytes in \(L\), and LF shifts all of a run's rows by the same amount. So LF is an interval exchange: a handful of intervals, each moved whole to a new place. The mathematical structure of inverse-BWT navigation sets out that structure. A new way back from the BWT shows Cells shrinking the exchange step by step on a three-byte block, and the technical companion describes its memory layout.

Wikipedia: Interval exchange transformation

An interval exchange transformation cuts an interval into pieces and puts them back in a different order, each piece moved whole, without stretching it. Here, LF does exactly this to the block's rows, one piece per run. Cells repeatedly shrinks the exchange onto a smaller interval, a step known as Rauzy induction, which has no Wikipedia article of its own.

The simplest correct picture. Cells shrinks LF's interval exchange from its right-hand end. At each stage it keeps a smaller set of rows. For each interval of kept rows it holds a return tower: the rows the LF path passes through before it comes back to a kept row. A tower has a width, the number of kept rows at its base, and a height, the number of LF steps from its base back to a kept row.
