It also has a word, the bytes those steps read, stored in forward text order. The towers' volumes, width times height, always add up to the block's rows. When the tower that holds bzip2's starting row closes on itself, its word is the block's text, and the starting row says where the text begins in it.

Wikipedia: Rokhlin lemma

A Kakutani–Rokhlin tower is a base set stacked with its successive images under a map, like the floors of a building. The Rokhlin lemma says that many systems can be cut almost entirely into tall towers, with a small piece left over. Here, the return towers are exact and finite: they cover the rows they describe with nothing left over.

Wikipedia: Free monoid

A free monoid is the set of all finite strings over an alphabet, the empty string included, combined by concatenation. Here, every word is an element of it: the bytes of one return path, in forward text order.

What we found.

  • Each of our working words names one exact object. The dictionary in section 2 gives them. Two need care: a letter labels an interval, and is neither a byte nor a word, and "per letter" in our figures means per original run, not per interval still alive.
  • Discrete Morse theory is an exact auxiliary model. It applies to the graph of LF's orbits, not to our memory records, and one step of Cells performs many of its row-level moves at once (section 3).
  • Cells is not a sheaf in the sense an earlier note claimed, but it is natural to make one. Our notes said the words are sections of a sheaf of monoids, without giving the sheaf. The exact object is simpler: a functor from LF's paths to words. Two genuine sheaves can then be built on top: one whose sections are the grammar's consistent evaluations (section 4), and one whose sections are exactly the places of the words in the text (section 5). Whether either buys anything in the decoder is an open question, not a claim.
  • Circular coordinates are exact, with one correction. Word places are consistent modulo the length \(d\) of the cycle being decoded. Modulo the block length \(n\) they are consistent only when LF is a single cycle through all \(n\) rows.
  • The formal account proves useful things (section 6): a correctness theorem for Cells, an algebraic check on every step, bounds on the number of steps, exact identities for batching steps, and exact certificates for reusing a path.

We label statements as the research records do. P marks a statement proved here under the hypotheses given. C marks a count reported in the project's records. H marks a hypothesis about what would help the decoder. We did not rerun the benchmarks for this post. We did check every formula in it on small blocks against a direct inverse BWT, in a short script.

Section 1 builds the towers and the step that shrinks them. Section 2 is the dictionary. Sections 3, 4 and 5 take Ghrist's three pictures in turn. Section 6 gives what the formulation proves, section 7 what the records count, and section 8 where it leaves us.

items.title: Towers, words and loops: a mathematical dictionary for BWT inversion
items.text:
Our BWT inversion is not the sheaf an earlier analogy suggested, yet the places of its words form one naturally.

16 November 2026 · 17 min read · Research synthesis

items.title: 1.1 The starting object: a permutation presented as an interval exchange
items.text:
Let

\[X=\{0,\ldots,n-1\},\qquad L\in\Sigma^n,\]

where \(\Sigma\) is the byte alphabet, \(L\) is the BWT's last column, and \(r_*\in X\) is bzip2's starting row (orig_ptr in its source). Define

\[C(c)=\#\{i:L[i]<c\},\]

and the LF permutation

\[\pi(x)=C(L[x])+\#\{i<x:L[i]=L[x]\}.\]

Wikipedia: Alphabet (formal languages)

An alphabet is the set of symbols that strings are written in. Here it is \(\Sigma\), the 256 possible byte values.

Wikipedia: Permutation

A permutation is a rearrangement of a finite set: each element is sent to exactly one place, and no place is left empty. Here, LF permutes the block's rows, and following it from one row reads the text backwards.

The output the reference inversion produces is

\[O[k]=L\!\left[\pi^{-(k+1)}(r_*)\right],\qquad 0\le k<n.\]

These are the inverse-BWT bytes, before bzip2's later run-length decoding.

On a maximal run of one byte, \(I_\alpha\), LF is a translation:

\[\pi(x)=x+\delta_\alpha,\qquad x\in I_\alpha.\]

Its image \(J_\alpha=\pi(I_\alpha)\) is another integer interval of the same width. So LF has a discrete interval-exchange presentation: the domain intervals in their order in \(L\), their image intervals in first-column order, and their widths.

The same formula extends to a real interval exchange on \([0,n)\), but here every length and translation is an integer. Cells uses an unnormalised, finite version of Rauzy induction, with cases for equal lengths and for closing a component. General results about minimal interval exchanges with irrational lengths do not automatically apply. The construction and its proof are in the construction's research journal, §§1–2.

items.title: 1.2 What is kept: a labelled first-return map
items.text:
At an intermediate stage the kept rows are

\[D_m=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}.\]

The active permutation is the first-return map

\[T_m(x)=\pi^{h_m(x)}(x),\qquad h_m(x)=\min\{j>0:\pi^j(x)\in D_m\}.\]

Wikipedia: Poincaré map

A first-return map, also called a Poincaré map, follows a system from a point of a chosen section until it first comes back to that section, and sends the point to where it lands; the number of steps taken is the return time. Wikipedia's article treats continuous flows. Here, the system is LF, the section is the kept rows, the return time is a tower's height, and the smaller map on the section is the induced system.

The kept rows are cut into intervals \(I_\alpha\) on which the return path is the same. Each interval has

\[\lambda_\alpha=|I_\alpha|,\qquad J_\alpha=T_m(I_\alpha),\qquad h_\alpha=h_m|_{I_\alpha},\]

and a byte word \(w_\alpha\). The orientation convention is the crucial one:

\[\boxed{L[x]\,L[\pi x]\cdots L[\pi^{h_\alpha-1}x]=\operatorname{rev}(w_\alpha)\quad(x\in I_\alpha).}\tag{1}\]

The stored word is the reverse of the bytes LF reads, so that it is already in forward text order. This is the construction's invariant I, and the code's comment on the stored words follows the same convention.

Two quantities must stay separate:

\[\lambda_\alpha=\text{number of base rows},\qquad h_\alpha=|w_\alpha|=\text{number of LF steps per return}.\]

A one-row interval can hold a very long word. Two intervals can hold identical words and still have different destinations.

items.title: 1.3 The towers are exact
items.text:
For each interval, take its levels

\[I_\alpha,\ \pi(I_\alpha),\ \ldots,\ \pi^{h_\alpha-1}(I_\alpha).\]

They form a finite return tower, also called a Kakutani–Rokhlin tower. Its base width is \(\lambda_\alpha\) and its height is \(h_\alpha\).

P. The levels of all the towers partition the saturation of the kept rows, the rows on LF cycles that meet them:

\[X_m=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}\pi^j(D_m).\]

Wikipedia: Orbit (dynamics)

An orbit is the set of states a system passes through from a starting point, by applying its map again and again. A permutation of finitely many rows has only cycles for orbits. Here, the saturation of the kept rows is the union of every LF cycle that meets them.

Every point of \(X_m\) has a unique most recent visit to \(D_m\) before it, and that visit gives its base point and its level. So

\[\boxed{\sum_\alpha \lambda_\alpha h_\alpha=|X_m|.}\tag{2}\]

When LF is one cycle through all \(n\) rows, the sum is always \(n\). If whole components without the starting row have been discarded, the sum is smaller.

This is the precise sense in which Cells keeps the original dynamics. Define the discrete suspension

\[\widehat X_m=\{(x,j):x\in D_m,\ 0\le j<h_m(x)\},\]

with the dynamics

\[\widehat T_m(x,j)=\begin{cases}(x,j+1),&j+1<h_m(x),\\(T_m(x),0),&j+1=h_m(x).\end{cases}\]

Then

\[\eta(x,j)=\pi^j(x)\]

is a bijection onto \(X_m\), and

\[\eta\circ\widehat T_m=\pi\circ\eta.\tag{3}\]

Wikipedia: Suspension (dynamical systems)

A suspension turns a map into a flow: each point rises for a while, set by a "roof" function, before it jumps to its image. Wikipedia describes the continuous version. The discrete suspension here does the same in whole steps, by stacking each kept row with the intermediate rows of its return path.

The towers, expanded, are conjugate to the original permutation on its saturation. The smaller map \(T_m\) on the bases is an induced system: it has fewer states and variable return times. Our notes on itinerary certificates (§3) described each step as a conjugacy of the smaller map to the larger one. That overstated it: the conjugacy holds once the tower levels are added, as (3) states.

Wikipedia: Topological conjugacy

A conjugacy is a change of coordinates that turns one system into another step for step, so that the two are the same system described differently. Here, the expanded towers are conjugate to LF on its saturation; the smaller induced map is not, until the tower levels are put back.

items.title: 1.4 One step
items.text:
Let \(A\) be the last domain interval and \(B\) the last image interval, with \(A\ne B\). Put

\[s=\min(\lambda_A,\lambda_B).\]

Their overlap at the end is

\[Q=I_A\cap J_B=[m-s,m).\]

The new kept set is \(D_{m-s}\). For

\[K=T_m^{-1}(Q)\subseteq I_B,\]

the old path has the form

\[x\in K\ \xrightarrow{B}\ T_m(x)\in Q\ \xrightarrow{A}\ T_m^2(x).\]

So the new return branch is

\[T_{m-s}|_K=T_m^2|_K,\]

with width \(s\), height \(h_B+h_A\), and stored word

\[\boxed{w_{\mathrm{new}}=w_Aw_B.}\tag{4}\]

LF passes through \(B\) and then \(A\); the stored word, in forward text order, is \(w_Aw_B\). On the block banana, one step has \(A\) and \(B\) of equal width one, \(w_A=\) a and \(w_B=\) b, and it made the word ab.

The updates to widths, words and the two orders follow directly from the two old returns crossing the removed end:

Case Width update Word update Order update \(\lambda_A>\lambda_B\) Shorten \(A\) by \(\lambda_B\) \(w_B\leftarrow w_Aw_B\) Move \(B\) just after \(A\) in image order \(\lambda_A<\lambda_B\) Shorten \(B\) by \(\lambda_A\) \(w_A\leftarrow w_Aw_B\) Move \(A\) just after \(B\) in domain order \(\lambda_A=\lambda_B\) Delete \(A\) \(w_B\leftarrow w_Aw_B\) \(B\) takes \(A\)'s place in image order

This is the table of the construction's journal (§2), which proves each case. When \(A=B\), something else happens: \(I_A=J_A\), so this branch is the identity and its tower closes.

items.title: 2. What do our words name?
items.text:
Each term of our working vocabulary names one of the objects above. Some name more than one, and the table says which.

Our term The mathematical object What to keep apart Letter A label \(\alpha\) for a base interval \(I_\alpha\), its image \(J_\alpha\), and their return data At first a run, possibly cut to isolate the starting row. It is neither a byte nor a word value. Word An element \(w_\alpha\in\Sigma^*\), the forward-text label of one return path The string value, its grammar node and one occurrence of that node are three different objects. Cell By context: the overlap \(Q\), the new return branch \(K\to T_m(Q)\), or the fixed record that holds that branch It is not a cell of a CW complex. Calling a step "a cell" is implementation language. Rule A production \(N\to UV\) in a binary straight-line program (SLP), or a node of a concatenation DAG A pair of child IDs is still a rule, even where the code calls it a compact "join". Induction step Replacing \(T_D\) by its first return to a smaller section \(D'\), with return labels composed The unequal cases are Rauzy moves. Equal-width reductions and closing components complete the finite algorithm. Marked row A distinguished original state \(r_*\), carried as a tower coordinate or as a distinguished terminal occurrence in the grammar Its row index is not its output position, and it need not stay the base point of its tower. Writer Evaluating the SLP, together with placing occurrences, scheduling copies, and choosing the cyclic phase The grammar's correctness and the writer's are separate obligations. Stop A stopping index in the induction's history, which selects an intermediate section and its labelled return map An early stop on a budget differs from a cycle closing naturally, and from refusing on a budget and falling back. It is not a critical cell.

The code says "cell" because a finished return piece is written into the records of both orders, while what remains of each interval stays at the fronts. That is a representation of the induction above, which the technical companion describes in detail.

Wikipedia: CW complex

A CW complex is a space built by gluing cells together: points (0-cells), then edges (1-cells), then discs and their higher-dimensional analogues. Our "cells" are not such cells. In section 3, though, the rows are 0-cells and the LF transitions are 1-cells.

Wikipedia: Formal grammar

A formal grammar is a set of rewriting rules, called productions, each saying how a symbol may be replaced by a string of other symbols. Here, every rule has the form \(N\to UV\): one symbol stands for the concatenation of two others.

Wikipedia: Straight-line grammar

A straight-line grammar, or straight-line program (SLP), is a grammar that produces exactly one string, never branching or looping. Repeated pieces are named once and reused, so the grammar can be far smaller than its string. Here, Cells' rules form one.

Wikipedia: Directed acyclic graph

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a set of nodes joined by one-way arrows, with no path that leads back to where it started. Here, each rule points to its two children, and children shared between rules make the grammar a DAG rather than a tree.

items.title: Substitutions, cylinders and grammar nodes
items.text:
Three further descriptions are useful.

A finite S-adic presentation. Each stage defines a substitution from the new alphabet of intervals into the previous one. Composed, they give a finite directive sequence of return-word substitutions. The stored object is most directly called an SLP. Versions matter: an assignment such as \(w_B\leftarrow w_Aw_B\) creates a new node that refers to the old values, so the grammar has no cycles.

Wikipedia: Symbolic dynamics

Symbolic dynamics studies a system through itineraries: for each point, the sequence of symbols naming the regions it visits. An S-adic presentation, which has no article of its own, builds such sequences by composing a series of substitutions, each replacing every symbol by a word. Here, each stage of the induction is one substitution.

Cylinder sets. A base interval lies inside a cylinder of constant return path. It need not be the largest cylinder for its byte word. Isolating the starting row deliberately cuts intervals finer, and equal byte words need not mean equal paths through the rows.

Wikipedia: Cylinder set

A cylinder set is the set of all sequences that agree on a fixed, finite stretch of positions, for instance all those whose first three symbols are given. Here, a cylinder is the set of rows whose return path follows a given itinerary.

Occurrence coordinates. A grammar node can occur many times in the output. The writer's "first place" for a node is the smallest position of one of its occurrences. It is not a position that belongs to the string value itself.

For an unrotated expansion of the root, the first places come from a min-plus computation over the DAG. If \(N\to UV\),

\[P(U)\leftarrow\min(P(U),P(N)),\qquad P(V)\leftarrow\min(P(V),P(N)+|U|).\tag{5}\]

That is why the writer passes over the rules in reverse order. Its next pass writes out factors and copies repeated occurrences, and its handling of the marked path adds the output phase (construction journal, §§3.2 and 3.5).

Wikipedia: Tropical semiring

The tropical semiring replaces ordinary addition by taking the minimum, and ordinary multiplication by addition, so that a "sum of products" becomes a "smallest total". Here, rule (5) is such a min-plus computation: a node's first place is the smallest of the places its parents offer.

items.title: 3. Is the induction discrete Morse theory?
What Ghrist states
items.text:
In §8.8 (pp. 205–206), a discrete vector field pairs cells \((\sigma,\tau)\), with \(\sigma\) a face of \(\tau\) of one dimension lower. Unpaired cells are critical. The field is a gradient when it has no periodic alternating flowline. The discrete flow is

Wikipedia: Discrete Morse theory

Discrete Morse theory simplifies a space built from cells by pairing cells off, each with a neighbour one dimension higher, and keeping only the unpaired, critical cells, without changing its homology. The pairing is a discrete vector field, and following it gives gradient paths. Here, each removed row pairs with its outgoing LF edge, and the gradient path from a kept row is its return path.

\[\Phi=\operatorname{Id}+\partial V+V\partial,\]

and Theorem 8.24 (p. 206) identifies the resulting Morse homology with the original cellular homology. These are constructions on chain modules, with signed or mod-two counts of paths.

Wikipedia: Homology (mathematics)

Homology counts the holes of a space in each dimension: its connected pieces, its loops, its enclosed cavities and so on. Cellular homology computes it from the cells of a complex. Here, every LF cycle is a circle, one piece with one loop, and a valid reduction must keep both.

Wikipedia: Chain complex

A chain complex is a sequence of chain modules, here formal sums of cells, linked by boundary maps that send each cell to its boundary; applying a boundary map twice gives zero. Homology is read off from it. Here, the Morse boundary in the table below is the boundary map of the reduced complex.

items.title: The exact construction for LF
items.text:
Build the orbit graph \(G_\pi\), with a vertex for every row \(x\) and an oriented edge \(e_x:x\to\pi(x)\). Every component is a circle. The complex is built from the dynamics; it is not the coordinate interval \([0,n)\). Subdivide one-point loops where needed, to meet Ghrist's hypothesis of a regular cell complex.

Choose a section \(D\) that meets every component under consideration, and define

\[\boxed{V=\{(y,e_y):y\notin D\}.}\tag{6}\]

That pairs each removed vertex with its outgoing edge.

P: no cycles. An alternating path follows LF through removed vertices. It must eventually reach \(D\), where it stops, so it cannot be periodic.

The correspondence, object by object:

Discrete Morse object In LF Original 0-cell A row Original 1-cell One LF transition Matched pair A removed row, paired with its outgoing transition Critical 0-cell A kept row \(x\in D\) Critical 1-cell The original outgoing edge \(e_x\) of a kept row Gradient continuation of \(e_x\) The path from \(x\) to its first return \(T_D(x)\) Morse boundary \(\widetilde\partial e_x=T_D(x)-x\)

The resulting Morse boundary is exactly the incidence boundary of the first-return orbit graph. One Cells step of width \(s\) performs \(s\) of these row-level eliminations together. That batching is the point: building the full matching row by row would throw away what the interval representation gains.

items.title: What does a stored word correspond to?
items.text:
A word is the byte coding of the return path, reversed as in (1). That is weaker than recording the path itself. Different paths can emit the same string, and one shared SLP node can stand for several path occurrences. The intervals and the marker keep distinctions that the string alone loses.

So it is legitimate to speak of Morse return paths decorated with word labels. "Morse theory with free-monoid coefficients" is not justified by the cited theorem. Its chain maps use addition and incidence coefficients, and the free monoid of strings is not a chain module. Ordered labels are an enrichment that needs its own argument for being preserved.

Two further qualifications. Suppressing vertices of degree two on a circle is a graph contraction, a Morse reduction. It is not literally a sequence of collapses through free faces inside the original circle, whose vertices each have two incident edges. And discarding a closed LF component without the starting row removes a whole circle, which does not preserve the homology of the full orbit graph. The Morse statement applies component by component to the components still represented.

Wikipedia: Edge contraction

An edge contraction removes an edge from a graph and merges its two ends into one vertex. Here, suppressing a removed row on an LF circle contracts one edge, and repeated contractions shorten the circle without breaking it.

items.title: What the theorem adds
items.text:
It gives a valid statement that homology is preserved, and it forces at least one critical vertex and one critical edge on every circle: a circle cannot be reduced to a point with its homology intact. It does not establish that the bytes are right, the output phase, the grammar's size, or the best order of contraction. Those depend on the labelled return invariant (1).

So the correspondence holds exactly, but between row-level contraction of return paths and a Morse matching, not between the implementation's records and topological cells. Our earlier note on Ghrist's book marked as proved that the induction is a Morse contraction with "flowlines labelled by words in the free monoid". That wording drops these distinctions.

items.title: 4. Are words sections of a sheaf?
What a sheaf here would require
items.text:
In §11.9 (p. 286), a cellular sheaf is a functor

\[\mathcal F:\operatorname{Face}(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal C.\]

Wikipedia: Sheaf (mathematics)

A sheaf attaches data to the pieces of a space, with rules saying how the data on overlapping or adjacent pieces must agree; a global section is a choice of data everywhere that obeys every rule. A cellular sheaf does this on the cells of a complex, with a stalk of data on each cell and a map for each face. Here, section 4 asks which sheaf, if any, our words form.

Wikipedia: Functor

A functor is a map between categories that sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows, keeping identities and composition. Here, the functor that matters sends each LF path to its word, and following two paths in turn to concatenating their words.

For \(\mathcal C=\mathbf{Mon}\), the category of monoids, that requires a monoid at every cell, a monoid homomorphism for every incidence of faces, and compatibility between those homomorphisms. Equation (11.3) on the same page describes the global sections as the limit of that diagram.

Wikipedia: Monoid

A monoid is a set with an associative way of combining two elements and an identity element that changes nothing. Strings under concatenation, with the empty string, form one, and so do the natural numbers under addition. A monoid homomorphism keeps the combining and the identity: word length is one.

Wikipedia: Limit (category theory)

A limit of a diagram is the most general object with compatible maps to every part of it: a universal way of making all the parts agree at once. Here, the global sections of a sheaf form such a limit.

A stored word is an element of a monoid. It is not itself a stalk. Our notes said that words are "free-monoid sections" of such a sheaf (the note on Ghrist's book, §0), but they never gave the stalks and incidence maps that claim needs.

The obvious choices do not work. Putting \(\Sigma^*\) on every cell, with identity restriction maps, would force adjacent cells to hold equal words, not to concatenate them. Nor can multiplication serve as a restriction map. For strings, which do not commute,

\[\mu:\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*,\qquad\mu(u,v)=uv\]

is not a homomorphism of the product monoid:

\[\mu((a,b)(c,d))=acbd,\qquad\mu(a,b)\mu(c,d)=abcd.\tag{7}\]

The difference matters precisely because order matters.

items.title: The exact object: a functor on paths
items.text:
Use the inverse-LF orientation, and label the induced edge

\[T_D(x)\longrightarrow x\]

by \(w_{\alpha(x)}\). Along paths, these labels concatenate in forward output order. That is a functor

\[\boxed{\mathsf{Path}(G_{T_D}^{-1})\longrightarrow B\Sigma^*,}\tag{8}\]

where \(B\Sigma^*\) is the category with one object, whose morphisms are words and whose composition is concatenation in traversal order: a path that takes \(e\) and then \(f\) is sent to \(w_e w_f\). (Under the usual convention that \(g\circ f\) means "\(f\) first", the target is the opposite monoid \((\Sigma^*)^{\mathrm{op}}\) instead.) It uses a monoid as a one-object category, which is a different construction from a sheaf valued in the category of monoids.

Wikipedia: Free category

A free category, or path category, is built from a directed graph: its arrows are the paths in the graph, and composing two arrows means following one path and then the other. Here, the path category of the return graph is where the functor (8) starts.

Wikipedia: Category (mathematics)

A category is a collection of objects and arrows between them that can be composed, with an identity arrow on each object. A monoid is exactly a category with one object: its elements are the arrows, and combining them is composition. Here, \(B\Sigma^*\) is the monoid of words seen this way.

The SLP stores compressed expressions for these path labels. Length is then a monoid homomorphism,

\[|\cdot|:\Sigma^*\longrightarrow(\mathbb N,+).\]

Together they account exactly for ordered word composition and for return times that add.

items.title: A genuine sheaf can be built
items.text:
For the grammar itself, we can build a sheaf of sets on a bipartite incidence graph. Each production has three distinct incidence edges, for its result, its left child and its right child, even when the two children are the same symbol, as in \(N\to UU\):

  • a symbol vertex has stalk \(\Sigma^*\);
  • a production vertex for \(N\to UV\) has stalk \(\{(u,v,w):w=uv\}\);
  • incidence edges have stalk \(\Sigma^*\);
  • the maps from a production to its edges are the matching projections;
  • the maps from a symbol to its edges are identities;
  • the terminals' values are fixed.

Wikipedia: Bipartite graph

A bipartite graph has two kinds of vertices, with edges only between the kinds, never within one. Here, the kinds are the grammar's symbols and its productions, and each edge records that a symbol takes part in a production.

Its global sections are the consistent evaluations of the grammar. It is an exact encoding, but it is extra formal structure, and it does not turn concatenation into a monoid homomorphism. There is also a particularly natural sheaf of positions, built in section 5.3.

The verdict. The monoid observation is sound and useful. "Words are free-monoid sections" does not follow until a sheaf is specified. Ghrist's section licenses such definitions; it supplies neither them nor a faster way to evaluate.

items.title: 5.1 The cocycle and its period
items.text:
Restrict attention to the selected LF cycle \(C\), the one through the starting row, of length \(d\). The induced cycle on \(D\cap C\) has return lengths \(h(x)\).

P. Its return paths partition \(C\), so

\[\sum_{x\in D\cap C}h(x)=d.\tag{9}\]

On the induced graph, orient edges in the LF direction and define

\[a(e_x)=-h(x),\qquad e_x:x\to T_D(x).\]

This is an integer 1-cocycle. On a graph every 1-cochain is a cocycle, because there are no 2-cells, so what carries the information is its period:

Wikipedia: Cocycle

A cocycle is a cochain, an assignment of numbers to the edges (or higher cells) of a space, that passes a closure test; on a graph every cochain passes. A coboundary is a cochain of the form "value at the head minus value at the tail" for some numbers on the vertices. Here, the step lengths form a cocycle that is not a coboundary, because round the cycle they add up to \(-d\), not zero.

\[\langle a,[C_D]\rangle=-d.\tag{10}\]

It follows that \(a\) is not the coboundary of an integer-valued or real-valued position function on the closed cycle. Modulo \(d\), though, it is exact:

\[\boxed{p(T_D(x))-p(x)\equiv-h(x)\pmod d.}\tag{11}\]

Here \(p(x)\) is the place in the text just after the word of \(x\). The scaled cocycle \(a/d\) is a real cocycle with integral period \(-1\), so it integrates to a coordinate in \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), and one marked occurrence fixes the additive phase. This is the exact link to §7.13 (pp. 185–186), and in particular to the correspondence between integral first cohomology and maps to the circle on p. 186.

Wikipedia: Cohomology

Cohomology measures when local data, such as a number on every edge, fail to come from one global quantity, such as a position for every vertex. The failure shows up as a nonzero total round a loop, called a period. Here, integral first cohomology classifies the ways of wrapping a space round a circle, which is how word places become circular coordinates.

Wikipedia: Modular arithmetic

Modular arithmetic is arithmetic on a clock: modulo \(d\), two numbers count as equal when they differ by a multiple of \(d\). Here, places taken modulo the cycle length \(d\) come back to their start after one trip round the cycle, which places as plain integers cannot.

Wikipedia: Circle group

The circle group \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) is the real numbers with only the part after the decimal point kept, so that 0.9 plus 0.2 is 0.1. A coordinate with values there wraps around instead of growing. Here, places in the text divided by \(d\) are such circular coordinates.

Keep the edge increments as well as the vertex coordinates. At final closure the induced graph may have one vertex and one loop, and the vertex's coordinate alone says nothing about how far the loop winds.

Wikipedia: Winding number

A winding number counts how many times a closed loop goes round a point or a circle, with direction. Here, the edge increments record how far round the circle each step goes, which a vertex's circular coordinate alone cannot show.

items.title: 5.2 Why modulo \(n\) is not always correct
items.text:
Stop and walk writes the invariant as

\[p(Tx)\equiv p(x)-|w(x)|\pmod n.\]

That is correct when LF is a single \(n\)-cycle. For a selected cycle of length \(d<n\), summing it once round the cycle would give

\[0\equiv-d\pmod n,\]

which is impossible. A concrete valid example is a periodic block:

\[\text{text}=\texttt{abab},\qquad L=\texttt{bbaa}.\]

Its LF permutation is

\[\pi=(0\ 2)(1\ 3).\]

No row-valued \(p:X\to\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\) satisfies \(p(\pi x)=p(x)-1\): either two-cycle would need \(0\equiv-2\pmod4\).

There are three precise ways out: take positions modulo the selected period \(d\); take positions on an occurrence cover that tells successive visits to the same physical row apart; or state the hypothesis that LF is a single \(n\)-cycle. For a valid periodic BWT input, the selected cycle is repeated to make \(n\) bytes. For an arbitrary column, the reference semantics likewise repeat the selected cycle and cut it to length.

The construction handles this (journal, §2). The stop-and-walk record assumes one \(n\)-cycle explicitly, in its §2. The post states that hypothesis two paragraphs after the formula, as "LF passes through every row of a block in one cycle", which holds for every Wikidata block we decode but not for a periodic one. Later shorthand should keep the hypothesis next to the formula.

items.title: 5.3 The position sheaf
items.text:
Here is a concrete realisation of the phrase "positions are sections of length data". For each induced edge \(e:x\to y\), put \(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z\) at both end vertices and at the edge. Give every edge two endpoint incidences, even when it is a loop (\(x=y\)), or subdivide loops first, so that a loop's two maps stay distinct. Then define the maps from the ends

\[\rho_{x,e}(u)=u-h_e,\qquad\rho_{y,e}(v)=v.\]

A global section satisfies

\[\rho_{x,e}(p(x))=\rho_{y,e}(p(y)),\]

which is exactly (11). These are maps of sets, or affine maps of torsors. In general they are not group or monoid homomorphisms, since translation by a nonzero constant does not preserve the identity.

Wikipedia: Principal homogeneous space

A torsor, also called a principal homogeneous space, is a set where differences between elements make sense but no element is singled out as zero, like positions on a line with no chosen origin. Here, the position sheaf's stalks behave as torsors: one marked occurrence chooses the origin.

Sections exist precisely when the total increment round each cycle vanishes modulo the chosen modulus. One anchor fixes the remaining additive freedom on each component. With the stalks and restriction maps that were missing, the compatibility claim becomes exact.

items.title: 5.4 What Example 7.37 contributes
items.text:
Example 7.37 (p. 185) comes just before the §7.13 heading. It uses the discrete Hodge decomposition of Theorem 7.34 (p. 184) to split pairwise comparison data into a gradient ranking and cyclic inconsistencies. For Cells, the relevant lesson is the obstruction to a real-valued ranking on a closed cycle with nonzero circulation.

Wikipedia: Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition

The Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition splits a flow into a part that comes from a potential and parts that circulate. On a graph of pairwise comparisons, it splits the data into a global ranking plus cyclic inconsistencies; this discrete form is the discrete Hodge decomposition Ghrist uses. Here, the nonzero circulation of the step lengths round an LF cycle is what rules out a real-valued ranking of positions.

The harmonic smoothing in §7.13 has no evident role in exact decoding. Replacing the length cocycle by a cohomologous harmonic representative keeps the winding, but in general it moves the positions given to intermediate vertices. Decoding needs the actual return lengths, not only their cohomology class.

Finally, the row coordinate \(p\) and the writer's first-occurrence function \(P\) in (5) are different objects. The first integrates lengths along an orbit; the second chooses canonical occurrences in a grammar DAG.

items.title: 6. What does the formal account prove?
6.1 A compact correctness theorem
items.text:
P. Suppose an implementation maintains:

  1. the first-return map on the kept section;
  2. the return-word invariant (1), exactly;
  3. a distinguished occurrence of \(r_*\) in the return towers;
  4. an SLP whose evaluation equals each stored return word.

Then the closure of the marked tower determines the reference inverse-BWT output.

Proof. Isolate \(r_*\) at the start as a base interval of its own, one row wide. The code does exactly this, cutting the starting row's run into up to three intervals. The marked base stays one row wide: an interval of width one can never be strictly wider than another positive integer width, so it is never the one shortened, and an equal step leaves the survivor one row wide.

When its branch closes, its return word \(E\) describes exactly the selected LF cycle. Let \(d=|E|\), and let \(j\) be the position of the marked terminal in \(E\). The reference walker steps through inverse LF before it emits, so its output is

\[\boxed{O[k]=E[(j+1+k)\bmod d],\qquad 0\le k<n.}\tag{12}\]

Equation (1) gives the bytes, the marker gives the phase, and repetition gives the requested length. ∎

This is stronger than a homology argument, because it keeps the observable and the distinguished occurrence. The writer still needs its own proof that the copies it schedules actually produce this string. One recorded bug shows the difference: an earlier writer left some bytes on the marked rules' path unwritten while the grammar was correct (technical companion, §3).

items.title: 6.2 Widths and heights transform dually
items.text:
For a top win (\(\lambda_A>\lambda_B\)), let \(M=I+E_{AB}\), with rows indexed by old intervals and columns by new ones. Then

\[\lambda_{\mathrm{old}}=M\lambda_{\mathrm{new}},\qquad h_{\mathrm{new}}=M^{\mathsf T}h_{\mathrm{old}}.\tag{13}\]

The first equation undoes the subtraction of widths; the second adds return times. Therefore

\[\lambda_{\mathrm{new}}^{\mathsf T}h_{\mathrm{new}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathsf T}h_{\mathrm{old}}.\]

That is a cheap algebraic check on every update. An equal step uses the corresponding rectangular incidence matrix. Either way, it states that the towers' volume is conserved, without following individual rows.

Wikipedia: Elementary matrix

An elementary matrix differs from the identity matrix by a single row operation, such as adding one row to another. Here, \(M=I+E_{AB}\) records one step: adding one interval's width back onto another's.

Wikipedia: Transpose

The transpose of a matrix swaps its rows and columns. When widths change by a matrix and heights by its transpose, the total of width times height stays the same, the algebra that keeps a dot product fixed. Here, that total is the towers' volume.

items.title: 6.3 Bounds on the present schedule of steps
items.text:
Let \(r_0\) be the number of starting intervals after the starting row is isolated, so \(r_0\le r+2\) for \(r\) runs. Let \(S\) count the ordinary concatenating steps. When LF is one \(n\)-cycle,

\[\boxed{r_0-1\le S\le n-1.}\tag{14}\]

P. Each step removes at least one kept row, which gives the upper bound. Only equal steps delete an interval, and a complete reduction ends with one interval, so there are exactly \(r_0-1\) equal steps. The lower bound needs changing when components without the starting row are discarded, or when the selected component closes before others.

No general \(O(r\,\mathrm{polylog}\,n)\) bound holds for the present subtraction schedule. For the primitive text, with the starting row not isolated,

\[T=(ab)^k a,\qquad n=2k+1,\]

the BWT has two runs, of widths \(k\) and \(k+1\), but the algorithm takes exactly

\[S=k+1=\frac{n+1}{2}\]

steps. After the first subtraction the widths are \(k\) and \(1\), and repeated subtractions of one finish the reduction. The construction journal's count of 449,991 steps at \(n=899{,}981\) (§§2 and 4) matches this formula.

The same family shows why long words must stay compressed. Successive return words grow linearly, so storing all of them literally can take quadratic total bytes.

Wikipedia: Big O notation

Big O notation describes how a quantity grows while ignoring constant factors: \(O(f)\) means at most a constant times \(f\) for large inputs, and the related \(\Omega(f)\) means at least. Here, it states bounds on the number of steps and on the work of producing the output.

items.title: 6.4 Some batching identities are proved; their speed benefit is not
items.text:
For \(q\) consecutive strict top wins by the same pair,

\[\lambda_A'=\lambda_A-q\lambda_B,\qquad w_B'=w_A^q w_B.\tag{15}\]

For \(q\) consecutive strict bottom wins,

\[\lambda_B'=\lambda_B-q\lambda_A,\qquad w_A'=w_Aw_B^q.\tag{16}\]

These identities are exact. Binary powering can represent \(w^q\) with \(O(\log q)\) extra SLP rules. Changes of order, the boundaries of equal steps, and the transport of the marker must also be composed correctly.

Wikipedia: Exponentiation by squaring

Exponentiation by squaring computes a power \(x^q\) with about \(\log_2 q\) multiplications, by squaring repeatedly and combining the squares that the binary digits of \(q\) pick out. Here, the same trick builds a word repeated \(q\) times with \(O(\log q)\) grammar rules.

H. Whether such acceleration speeds up the actual decoder depends on how often suitable streaks occur and what finding them costs. The identities do show that the topology does not force one operation per elementary subtraction.

items.title: 6.5 Exact itinerary certificates
items.text:
Suppose a piecewise translation \(F\) follows the intervals

\[I_{i_0},\ldots,I_{i_{k-1}},\]

with cumulative translations \(s_0=0,s_1,\ldots,s_k\). Then

\[\boxed{J=\bigcap_{j=0}^{k-1}(I_{i_j}-s_j)}\tag{17}\]

is exactly the set of starts that follow that itinerary.

P. For \(x\in J\), the \(j\)-th state is \(x+s_j\in I_{i_j}\), by induction on \(j\). Every such start emits the same sequence of words and finishes at \(x+s_k\). This is a deterministic certificate for reusing a path, and it needs no hashing.

A later induced interval lies inside the matching certificate, but it need not equal the largest one. The certificates record's lemma states containment, correctly; its title's stronger wording, that the coarser exchange's intervals are "exactly" those columns, needs that qualification. A composite map being a translation does not by itself prove a constant itinerary, either: different itineraries can have the same net translation. The return partition that Cells maintains supplies the missing premise.

items.title: 6.6 What lower bounds are actually available
items.text:
Producing \(n\) bytes explicitly needs \(\Omega(n)\) byte traffic, so in a model that charges per byte the output costs \(\Omega(n)\). It does not need \(n\) dependent LF loads, \(n\) grammar rules or a serial ranking walk. Similarly, producing an explicit position for every kept row needs space and work for those values; an algorithm that avoids that representation solves a different problem.

Our records' arguments about what memory must be kept say that occurrences not yet placed need recoverable expansion information (the census of word lifetimes, §4). They do not prove that this information must sit in the present layout of rules and arena. Re-encoding, recomputation, other grammars and other placement strategies remain possible. The compact tail grammar is a concrete example: it keeps the same grammar and changes how it is stored.

items.title: 7. What do the records count?
items.text:
These are reported counts, separate from the proofs above, each with its scope:

Status Recorded result Scope C 27,439,723 elementary steps, \(S/r=1.812\), \(S/n=0.1309\) (construction journal) The original right-end census on 233 Wikidata blocks; not an asymptotic law C At a stop after \(1.5r\) cells, about 33%, or 5.0 bytes per original run, of word storage avoided (stop and walk, reopened) A prototype's counts; separate from timing the whole decoder C Compact tail from \(1.2r\): 4.89 bytes per original run saved, about 32% of word storage (compact tail) All 233 Wikidata blocks, with wider IDs where needed; the same grammar C At \(\beta=1.5\), at least about one third of sampled starts share a whole-word itinerary covering 256 bytes with another start, certified within a 64-step search that does not wrap past the walk's end. This is a lower bound: starts the search doesn't certify are not shown to fail (on b a^999 the true share is 0.744 and this search reports 0) (certificates) Every eighth Wikidata block; does not show that all this reuse can be realised profitably

Here \(\beta\) is the stop's budget of cells per original run. One vocabulary correction changes how these figures read: "per letter" in our records usually means per original run \(r\), not per interval still alive. The record on splitting the walk gives, at \(\beta=1.5\), approximately

\[m=0.672r,\qquad q_{\mathrm{live}}=0.1212r,\]

so there are about 5.54 kept points per live interval, not 0.672.

Likewise, "the stop is free" means that the kernel's existing budget check can be reused. Building the snapshot and emitting from it still cost work. "One lane is needed" is an engineering judgement, not a mathematical consequence of the number of points. The early prototype also leaves the shift of phase for the original row unexercised or uncounted, so its byte comparisons should not be promoted into a proof for every starting row and for periodic input (stop-and-walk post, §3; reopened design, §3).

items.title: 8. Where this leaves us
items.text:
The strongest conclusion the evidence warrants has four parts. Labelled first-return towers and SLP evaluation give Cells its correctness proof. Discrete Morse theory gives an exact auxiliary model of the reduction. Circular cohomology describes the phase compatibility precisely, once the modulus is the selected cycle's length. And the monoid-sheaf claim needed a construction, which sections 4 and 5.3 now supply.

None of the cited sections of Ghrist's book establishes that the decoder is optimal. A claim that continuing the induction is the only cheap way to recover positions would need a specified representation and cost model, and then a lower-bound argument. The records give useful design comparisons and counts, but no such impossibility theorem.

What comes next follows from the status of each part. The two sheaves of sections 4 and 5.3 are exact, and whether either suggests a cheaper way to place words (H) is untested. The batching identities (15) and (16) are proved; whether streaks are common and cheap enough to find for them to pay (H) is a question for a count. The check (13) costs a multiply-add per step and could be added to the debug checks as it stands.

Sources:

  • R. Ghrist, Elementary Applied Topology, edition 1.0, Createspace, 2014. Page numbers are those of the printed edition: §7.13 (pp. 185–186), Theorem 7.34 (p. 184), Example 7.37 (p. 185), §8.8 and Theorem 8.24 (pp. 205–206), §11.9 and equation (11.3) (p. 286). §8.8 (p. 205), §11.9 (p. 286) and §7.13 (p. 185) have been checked against the book; the other page numbers and Theorem 7.34 have not yet.
  • The construction and its proof: the construction's research journal, and the code.
  • Stop and walk: the design record and its reopening; the census of word lifetimes.
  • In review as research pull request #497: splitting the walk, the compact tail, itinerary certificates and the note on Ghrist's book.

Further reading, in a suggested order:

  1. Interval exchange transformation: how LF is presented, and the setting for Rauzy-style induction.
  2. Rokhlin lemma: the tower viewpoint, for its construction rather than its measure theory.
  3. Free monoid and straight-line grammar: how return paths become strings, and how repeats compress.
  4. Discrete Morse theory: the same reduction, seen as eliminating matched cells.
  5. Functor and sheaf: path concatenation is functorial, and compatible placements are sections of a sheaf.
  6. Cohomology and cocycle: why positions are circular, and why the cycle's length matters.

items.title: Stop and walk
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

Stop and walk is a new way for mibz2 to finish rebuilding a block of text. It stops the rebuild partway, walks once round the small loop that is left, and writes the text out as it goes. The rebuild never makes the pieces of text its last steps would have built: a third of them, for about 2% more instructions. It did not ship. On our 10-core test machine it ran slightly slower, because the walk waits on one memory load after another, and those waits cost more time than the smaller memory saved.

How it works, step by step. mibz2's Cells kernel rebuilds a block by shrinking a map of it, one step at a time. Each step builds a longer piece of the text, a word. The full rebuild can't put any word in the output until near its end. So it keeps every word until then. Stop and walk stops partway instead, after 1.5 steps for every run of equal bytes in the block. That leaves one small loop of points. One point on it has a known place in the output. Walking round the loop from that point puts each point's word next to the one before. So the words the last steps would have built never get made.

Why that could make mibz2 faster. Fewer words mean less memory per block. That matters where many threads share one cache. Our test machine is an Intel i9 with 10 cores. Since mibz2 0.5.1, it decodes one block per thread at every thread count. From 8 threads up, mibz2 switches to the lazy-letters version of Cells. Before 0.5.1, the highest thread counts ran teams of threads sharing one block, and memory cuts to Cells never reached them. Now a cut to the lazy kernel reaches every count from 8 to 20 (section 5).

Where it stands. We built stop and walk, and it gives the same bytes as the shipped kernel. We counted its instructions and timed it on the i9. It did not meet the rule we set before the timing, so mibz2 keeps the shipped kernel (section 6).

The rest of the opening gives the background the idea rests on.

The BWT, in brief. mibz2 is our bzip2 decoder, written in Rust. bzip2 compresses text in blocks of up to 900 kB. It stores each block as the last column of the block's sorted rotations: the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT). To undo it, a decoder follows a map, LF, from row to row of the sorted block, one byte per row. Within a run, a stretch of equal bytes in that column, LF moves every row by the same amount. So the map is one shifted interval per run, not one entry per row (the post of 8 November).

Cells. Cells shrinks that map step by step, and records each step as a word. Each step deletes rows that the path through the block can only pass through, and gives an interval a longer word to stand for the bytes it skipped. The code calls an interval a letter and each step a cell. When one letter is left, its word is the whole block, and a final pass, the writer, expands it into bytes. The technique is Rauzy–Veech induction (the technical companion), and section 1 runs it by hand on a three-byte block.

What the kernel keeps. It keeps two things while it works. The first is the letters' bookkeeping: their lengths, links and places. Hand-me-down slots and smaller second-order slots trimmed it, and lazy letters then cut its slots from 20 bytes a letter to 6.4. The second is the words. The kernel stores a word of up to 16 bytes as its bytes, and a longer one as a 16-byte rule naming its two halves. Those word bytes average 15.6 a letter on mibz2's Wikidata benchmark, an 11.9 MB extract of a Wikidata dump that decompresses to 210 MB. The lazy kernel touches 29.5 bytes a letter besides its output, so the words make up about half (the ring's record). No change so far has cut them.

The numbers. On Wikidata a block's rebuild takes about 1.8 steps a run in all, so stopping at 1.5 leaves out about the last fifth. At the stop, the loop has about one point for every 22 rows of the block.

items.title: Stop and walk: cutting a BWT inversion short and walking the rest
items.text:
Halting each block's rebuild early spares mibz2 a third of the text pieces it stores, but on ten cores the slower walk outweighs the memory saved.

16 November 2026 · 17 min read · Research result

items.title: What was found
items.text:
The takeaways, each shown in a section below:

  • The kernel never makes a third of the word bytes. Stopping at 1.5 cells a run leaves 33% of the word bytes unmade. That is 5.0 bytes a letter, counted by a prototype on all 233 large Wikidata blocks. The saving comes to about a sixth of everything the lazy kernel touches. The timing showed the relief indirectly, as less extra processor time at 10 threads (section 2, section 4, section 6).
  • The walk writes each word once and copies it after. It goes once round the loop, one point at a time. The walk expands a long word where it first meets its letter, and every later point copies it from there. The built kernel gives the same bytes as the shipped one on all 431 blocks of the Wikidata extract (section 3).
  • It costs 10 to 12 instructions a letter. Over the whole decode, that adds about 2% to the shipped decoder's instructions. The build had to stay under +20 a letter, and it does. On one thread its kernel runs about 10% slower, because the walk waits on one memory load after another. A cloud machine took that timing, so it hints at speed and proves nothing (section 4).
  • It did not ship. On the 10-core i9 it ran 1% to 1.5% slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads, and we detected no difference at 10 and 12. The memory relief was real, but with one worker a core the walk's waits outweighed it. It could only have replaced the lazy kernel everywhere that kernel runs, and never had a thread range of its own (section 6).

Run to the end, or stop at 1.5 cells a run and walk

Run to the end: the lazy kernel todayevery word is held until the last step, when the words' places become knowncells made0all of them, about 1.8 a runword bytes held100%Stop and walkstop once 1.5 cells a run are made; what is left is one loop of pointscells madenever runstop: 1.5 a runword bytes held67%never made: 33%Then walk the loop once12345678start: place knowncopy: the same letter again12345678the block's text, written from its end back to its start, in one passa bead's colour is its letter; its word ends where the last bead's word began Above and middle: conceptual bars, with counted figures. Wikidata's blocks need about 1.8 cells a run in all; stopping at 1.5 leaves 33% of the word bytes unmade (a prototype's count over 233 blocks). Below: the analogy. Each bead is a point of the map left at the stop, its colour is the letter it belongs to, and the letter's word is the bead's piece of text. The real loop has about one point for every 22 rows. The analogy stops holding for the induction itself: it does not thread beads one at a time, but deletes whole intervals of points at each step, under one rule per letter.

Where things stand. We built stop and walk as test variants of the lazy kernel and timed them on the i9 from 8 threads to 20 (#493). Under the rule we set before the run, stop and walk is not adopted, and mibz2's default stays as it was. Section 6 has the figures. The test variants stay on their branch.

items.title: 1. How does Cells rebuild a block?
items.text:
This post uses these terms, each worked through on an example below:

Term What it is in mibz2 run a stretch of equal bytes in the BWT's last column letter an interval of rows that the map moves as one; at first, one run word the bytes a letter's interval stands for; one byte at first, longer as the rebuild goes on cell the overlap of an interval in one order with an interval in the other; each step makes one induction replacing the map by a smaller one that skips some rows, while recording their bytes in words rule a long word kept as its two halves, such as X = AB, each an existing word

Take the three-byte block aab. Its rotations, sorted, are aab, aba and baa, so its last column reads baa. That column has two runs: b in row 0 and aa in rows 1 and 2. Call them B and A. LF sends each row to the row of the rotation one byte earlier. It sends B's row to row 2. It sends A's two rows to rows 0 and 1, shifting both by the same amount. Followed from row 0, LF visits row 2, then row 1, then row 0 again. That is one cycle through every row, and it reads the block's bytes backwards.

The block aab as two intervals and one cycle

The block aab, its rotations sortedrowrotationlast byte0aabb1abaa2baaaThe runs as intervals, and where LF sends themlast columnafter LFB: row 0 · bA: row 1 · aA: row 2 · arow 0row 1row 2A shifts by −1B shifts by +2LF visits row 0 → row 2 → row 1 → row 0: one cycle through every row. Each run moves as one interval,so the map is two shifted intervals, and a step of the rebuild looks only at their ends. Worked by hand. On the left, the sorted rotations and their last bytes. On the right, the two runs as intervals, in the last column's order and in the order LF lands them. Moving the intervals around without reversing any of them is what makes this an interval exchange. Section 1 of the Cells post runs the same block.

One step of the induction. Look at the right-hand end of both orders. In the last column, the last interval is A, two rows long. Among the places LF lands, the last is row 2, where B lands. B is the shorter, and it lands inside A, at A's end. Nothing else reaches row 2, and from row 2 the path always goes on to row 1. So the step can delete row 2, as long as it keeps its byte. B's word grows from b to ab: A's a followed by B's own b, in the order the rebuild records them. Both intervals are now one row long, and the map is 0 → 1 → 0.

One step: row 2 goes, its byte stays in B's word

Before: three rows, three moves of LF0word b2word a1word aOnly B lands on row 2,and from row 2 the pathalways goes on to row 1.After one step: row 2 deleted, its byte kept in a longer word0word ab1word aone move now covers twoB: one row, word abA: one row, word a2 + 1 bytes: the block Worked by hand, on the block aab. The smaller map skips row 2, and loses nothing: B's word now holds its byte. Each move of the smaller map stands for the run of moves of the old one that it skips, which is what a first-return map means.

On a real block each step does the same at the right-hand end. It deletes a whole interval's worth of rows at once and records the new word. The kernel records a long word as a rule naming its two halves, so it costs 16 bytes whatever its length. When only one letter is left, its word is the whole block. On aab one more step would finish it. A and B now have the same length, so they join into one letter whose word is aab.

The rule that makes the walk possible. Moving along the smaller map moves through the text by exactly the length of the word that move stands for. If \(p(x)\) is the place in the block of the text at point \(x\), \(T\) is the smaller map, and \(w_\alpha\) is the word of the letter \(\alpha\) that holds \(x\), then

\[ p(T(x)) \equiv p(x) - |w_\alpha| \pmod n , \]

where \(n\) is the block's length. The word \(w_\alpha\) lies just below \(p(x)\) in the text, and \(T(x)\) starts where it ends. On aab after one step, point 0 holds the two bytes ab and point 1 holds a. Going round the loop once moves through 2 + 1 = 3 bytes, the whole block. The design's record proves this as its invariant I. It holds at every stage of the induction, not only at its end.

items.title: 2. Why does the rebuild hold its words to the end?
items.text:
To put a word in the output, the writer needs its place: the offset in the block where its bytes begin. Cells learns places from one row only. bzip2 records which row of the sorted block holds the original text's first rotation. Cells keeps that row marked, as a letter of its own. The kernel can fix a word's place only once the word has become part of the word around that row. In Cells' order of steps, that word grows only in the last steps, so until then it knows almost no word's place.

That has a direct consequence for memory. A census of every word followed each word from when the kernel made it until nothing needed it. It covered Wikidata's 233 blocks of at least 65,536 rows. It found that the writer still needs 72% of the word bytes when the induction ends. The other 28% die earlier. A short word that every longer word built from it has copied is dead once its letter no longer holds it.

The kernel can't give those 28% back cheaply. A dead word almost never sits at the top of the store. Its letter kept it for a long time, while the kernel added other words above it. A store that only frees from the top, the cheapest kind, reclaims none of them on any block. Reclaiming them needs a free list or a compaction pass, which is bookkeeping for every letter, in a loop that is already short of registers. Writing words out early doesn't help either. The writer can't write a word before it knows the word's place, and it learns places only at the very end.

So the census closed with a lower bound. While places come only from that one row, the kernel has to keep every word not yet inside the word around it. In Cells' order that is the writer's whole set of words until the last step, which is exactly what the kernel holds. The words weren't too big; the kernel just didn't know their places yet. The one way out the census named was to learn places some other way: by walking.

items.title: 3. How can a walk place the words?
items.text:
Stop the induction early, and it leaves a smaller map of the same kind. It has a set of points, each belonging to a letter, and a rule for moving from a point to the next. Because LF passes through every row of a block in one cycle, the smaller map also forms one loop through all its points. The rule of section 1 says each move round the loop passes over exactly one letter's word. So once the walk knows one point's place, the word lengths give every other place.

The walk does know one point's place. The design's record proves that the mark on bzip2's starting row always stays on an interval one row long. So at the stop the mark sits on a single point. Its place follows from the row's offset within its word, which the writer already finds. The stopped map still holds everything the rebuild needs. It records where each letter's intervals lie in both orders, each letter's word and its length, and the mark. The induction has discarded nothing; it has only changed how it describes the text.

Two ways to finish. On aab, after one step, ordinary Cells would take the second step and then expand aab. Stop and walk instead stops there and walks the two points.

Two ways to finish aab

Run to the endone more step joins the two lettersA and B, now of equal length, joinone letter, word aab: the whole blockthe writer expands it into the outputevery word is held until this pointStop and walkstop after one step, then walk the two pointsa0a1b231. point 0, place 3: ab ends there2. point 1, place 3 − 2 = 1: a ends there3. back to point 0, place 1 − 1 = 0: done Worked by hand. The places follow the rule of section 1: each point's word ends at its place, and the next point's place is this one's less the word's length. Here the walk starts at point 0 for the illustration; in the kernel it starts at the marked point.

The walk in the kernel. The built kernel, in #493, walks the loop once. It follows the map forwards from the marked point and moves down the output. It writes each point's word so that the word ends at the point's place. After as many points as the loop has, it is back at the marked point, one block lower, and it has written the whole block. If the loop closes too early, or the bytes don't add up to the block, the kernel decodes the block again the shipped way.

Expand once, then copy. A letter's interval may hold many points, and each has the same word. Expanding a long word from its rules at every point would repeat the same work. An earlier version did just that, and its writing pass cost about twice the shipped writer's instructions. The walk expands a long word the first time it meets its letter, and notes where it wrote it. Every later point of that letter copies the bytes from there, so the output itself serves as a store of words already expanded. The walk copies a short word, kept as bytes, straight from where the induction stored it. The copy is a fixed 32 bytes, then 16 at a time for a longer word, so the walk doesn't branch on a word's length.

Writing abracadabra from a loop of four points

The loop, from the known pointXZYXX = abra, Y = ca, Z = d(made up, not a real block)place01234567891011abracadabra1. X, first time: expand2. Z3. Y4. X again: copy from 7–10copy from the first Xstep 1's wide store may reach below its word, into places not yet writtenThe walk goes down the output: each word ends where the last one began, so the first X lies above every copy. Conceptual: a made-up loop, not a real block's. The walk moves down the output, so it writes the first X (places 7 to 10) before, and above, the copy at 0 to 3. In a real block the loop has about one point for every 22 rows.

Why the wide stores are safe. A 32-byte copy of a 4-byte word writes 28 bytes too many. They land below the word, at places the walk hasn't reached yet, because places only fall as it goes. The walk writes each of those bytes again, correctly, when it gets there. A copy's source is always the first occurrence, which lies wholly above, so the walk finished it before reading it. Two places break that rule: place 0, where the walk wraps round the block, and the walk's last 32 bytes, just above where it began. There the walk writes each word exactly.

The only new table the walk needs is one 4-byte first place for each letter alive at the stop, about a tenth of the letters. As we first built it, we sized its tables to every letter, and they added about 20% to the peak memory of a worker, the thread that decodes a block. Before any timing, we cut them to the live letters. Locally the peak now matches the shipped kernel's: 37 against 37 MB on one thread, 83 against 85 on four (the revised rule).

Why one lane. An earlier design split the walk into eight lanes, so that their waits on memory overlapped. That needed an extra pass to measure each lane's stretch of the output first. And one lane's wide stores could overwrite bytes that a neighbouring lane had already written. A single ordered walk needs neither the extra pass nor any guard at the boundaries. It pays with a single chain of dependent loads, which section 4 comes back to.

items.title: 4. Where should it stop, and what does it cost?
items.text:
The stop needs a test, and the induction's inner loop has no room for one. That loop already uses more values than the processor has registers. An earlier version tested the map's remaining size on every cell. That test alone cost about 10 instructions a cell, whether the block stopped or not, and cancelled what the stop saved. So this design puts the stop on a count the kernel already keeps. The kernel refuses any block that would take more cells than a budget allows, so it counts every cell down already. Stopping after ⌈β r⌉ cells, where r is the block's number of letters at the start, needs only a different starting count. The design priced that at nothing. In the build, the cleanest form of it spilled the counter to memory and cost 16 to 38 instructions on every cell. So the build compares the counter with a stored bound instead. That costs about 2 instructions a cell.

We set the stop as β r cells, not as a size of the map. The kernel knows r before the induction starts, but not the total number of cells. On Wikidata a block takes 1.29 to 2.08 cells a run in all. Early in the induction most of the map disappears cheaply. Late in it few rows are left, but each step still makes a long word. Stopping earlier saves more words and leaves more points to walk, so β = 1.5 is a compromise read off the counts, not an optimum. Our prototype counted three settings over the 233 large blocks:

β (cells a run at the stop) blocks that stop map left, as a share of the rows (median) points walked a letter word bytes never made 1.4 232 of 233 0.082 1.23 43% (6.5 B a letter) 1.5 232 of 233 0.046 0.66 33% (5.0 B) 1.6 232 of 233 0.022 0.34 23% (3.4 B)

A block that takes fewer cells than β r never stops, and the kernel rebuilds it as before. The table shows the striking thing. By the stop at 1.5, the map has shrunk to under a twentieth of the rows. Yet a third of the word bytes are still to come. The count measured word storage, the rules and the stored bytes. It is not the process's memory, and we have not measured any drop in memory traffic or cache misses.

What it costs. The prototype predicted that stopping at 1.5 would save about 20 instructions a letter against the shipped kernel. The kernel's count, over the whole decode of the Wikidata extract with callgrind, an instruction counter, came out the other way. A letter here is one run of the 11,090,867 in the blocks Cells takes, and the whole decode costs about 550 instructions a letter. Before any timing, the team set a limit of +20 instructions a letter, under 4% of the decode.

β whole decode, first passing build a letter, against the shipped lazy kernel a letter, on the build the i9 run uses shipped 6.076 G instructions 1.4 6.360 G +25.6 +27.3 1.5 6.196 G +10.8 +12.3 1.6 6.154 G +7.0 +8.1

β = 1.5 stays under the limit. The counter itself varies by about 10 a letter between builds of the same source. So the count shows that β = 1.5 stays under the limit, not that it costs exactly 11 or 12 instructions. The two builds' figures agree within that noise.

The trade: word bytes never made, against instructions added

counted in the kernel (bar: ±10 of build noise)modelled from the prototypelimit: +200%10%20%30%40%−40−200+20+40instructions a letter added to the whole decode, against the shipped lazy kernelword bytesnever madeβ = 1.4β = 1.5β = 1.6+27.3+12.3+8.1 Counted and modelled, not timed. The heights, the share of word bytes never made, are a prototype's counts over the 233 large Wikidata blocks. The filled points are the built kernel's whole-decode instruction counts on the build the i9 run uses (the first passing build counted +25.6, +10.8 and +7.0); the hollow ones are what the design's model predicted, including the cost of reading the stopped map.

The count also shows where the prediction went wrong. At β = 1.5, on the first passing build, three costs differ. The cells never made were the cheap ones. The tail of the induction reads no new runs, so each of its cells costs about 38 instructions, not 71. Skipping them saves 13.2 a letter, not 21.5. The walk costs 52.1 instructions a letter, against the shipped writer's 49.5. The prototype's standalone walk cost 38.3. Each point takes about 31 instructions of fixed work: a rank lookup, a bit count and a read of the letter's record. Expanding each letter's first occurrence adds 14.6 a letter. And reading the stopped map into the walk's tables costs 18.9, not the 10 the model allowed. About 6,000 letters are alive in a block at the stop, and the kernel reads each twice.

Time on one thread. On a cloud machine, with the kernel's phases timed, β = 1.5 was about 10% slower than the shipped kernel. The walk runs about the writer's instructions in about twice the writer's time. Its step from one point to the next is a load, a bit count, a second load and an add. That takes about 20 cycles, and each step needs the one before it. That machine's timings prove nothing about speed; the i9 later measured 6.4% (section 6). They did say what the decisive run had to show: that when many threads share the cache, the bytes saved buy back more than the walk costs. A second lane, walking the other way round the loop, would halve the chain, but needs more tables, so it waits on the result.

Why the design is this way. An earlier version of stop and walk made the two mistakes this design avoids. It tested the map's size on every cell, which cost about as much as the stop saved. And it expanded each long word from its rules every time it appeared. Together they made it about 97 instructions a letter dearer than the shipped kernel, far over the limit. The figure sets its costs against this design's, item by item. The team now asks every failed build for that item-by-item list and sends it back to the design's author (§11a of its protocol).

Why the design is this way: an earlier version against this one, in instructions a letter

earlier version, stopped at a 32nd of the rowsthis design, stopped at 1.5 cells a runlimit +20−200+30+60+90cells never madethe tail of the induction−19−13.2the stop teston every cell+18about 2 a cell, in “the rest”writing the textpass 2 or the walk, less the writer's 49.5+54 (104 in all)+2.6 (52.1 in all)pass 1measuring each stretch+16removedreading the stopped mapwith ranking the starts, in the first+11+18.9zeroing scratchfor writing words exactlyabout +12not listedthe restthe total less the terms above+5+2.5total+97+10.8 Counted with callgrind over the whole decode of the Wikidata extract, in instructions per run of the blocks Cells takes, against the shipped lazy kernel; this design's figures are from its first passing build. The two builds stop at different points, a 32nd of the rows and 1.5 cells a run, so the rows compare designs, not one stop. “The rest” is each total less its listed terms, worked out here, not counted. The earlier version's two largest avoidable costs, the stop test and writing the text, are the two this design removes.

Why stop only once. A follow-up record, in review as #492, tried stopping again, on the walk's own tail. It gives the right bytes, but describing each extra level of the map costs about as much as the words it saves. The best two-stop version saves 1.3 bytes a letter more, for about 16 to 26 more instructions a letter. The single stop at 1.5 stays the design.

What is known, and how. The records label each statement as proved, counted or modelled:

Status What the records support Proved the stopped map keeps every path and its words; one loop with one known place gives every place; an ordered walk with first-place copies never overwrites a byte still needed Counted or tested a third of the word bytes never made at β = 1.5 (prototype, 233 blocks); +10.8 and +12.3 instructions a letter (kernel, callgrind); the same bytes as the shipped kernel on all 431 Wikidata blocks, the test files and 4,000 random columns Measured on the i9 slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads, level at 10 and 12; 5% less extra processor time from 1 thread to 10; 6.4% slower on one thread; faster with two workers forced onto each core Modelled whether the cache's size, its misses or the bandwidth to memory limit it; what a second lane would save Not done yet the Miri and fuzz runs, the mutation pass and the review of the new unsafe code, which the records list as owed before any adoption

items.title: 5. Why test it now?
items.text:
The kernel's bytes matter only where threads compete for the cache. On one thread, instructions decide the time. That is why lazy letters lost at 4 and 6 threads and won from 8. So the question is which thread counts run the lazy kernel, and until recently the answer was few of them. Why mibz2 stops scaling found the knee: past about 8 threads, each block decoded at once slowed the others. mibz2 answered with teams of threads that share one block: three teams of three at 10 threads. Those teams were later pipelined, and later still given a pit crew of two service threads for each block's serial steps. Those teams ran their own kernel, so Cells' memory cuts reached only 8 threads and below.

That changed in 0.5.1. #462 gave each of 10 threads a block of its own, decoded with lazy letters. #468 covered machines with 8 to 10 physical cores asked for more threads than that. They run one lazy worker a core, and leave the second hardware threads idle. The thread plan in the code, plan_with, now runs on the 10-core i9 as follows:

Threads asked for What runs 1 to 7 a worker a thread, eager Cells 8 to 10 a worker a thread, lazy letters 11 to 20 10 workers, one a core, lazy letters

Teams now run only on other machines. A machine with 6 or 7 physical cores gets teams of two when asked for more threads than it has cores. So does a machine with 11 cores or more, asked for 11 threads or more. Where the machine's topology can't be read, which includes every system other than Linux, mibz2 runs a worker a thread at every count.

The release ledger shows why that matters. It lists, for each release, which merge moved which thread count on the i9 by 3% or more. From 0.2.4 on, 10 to 20 threads moved in only three ways. Two changed how mibz2 grouped its threads: the teams, then pipelining them. One was an existing kernel ported to the teams. The third was 0.5.1's move onto Cells, which sped up 10 threads by 7.3%. Each of Cells' memory cuts, from the 20-byte slot to lazy letters, sped up only 8 threads or fewer, because teams ran above that. Now a cut to the lazy kernel's working set reaches every count from 8 to 20. Stop and walk trades instructions for memory, the trade lazy letters won and a ring of shared buffers lost. The ring cut the lazy kernel's bytes by 15% for 13% more decoder instructions. It ran slower at 8 threads and level at 9 and 10. By the prototype's count, stop and walk would cut 5.0 of those 29.5 bytes a letter, about a sixth, for about 2% more instructions.

items.title: 6. What did the timing show?
items.text:
We timed it on the i9, #493, under a rule we fixed before the data. The test decoder kept the shipped decoder's workers, thread plan and window of blocks in flight, and swapped only the kernel. It decoded four copies of the Wikidata extract at 8, 9, 10, 12 and 20 threads. Each of its ten paired rounds ran the shipped kernel and the three settings of β. At each count, β = 1.5 counts as faster if the 95% interval of its wall-time ratio lies wholly below 1. It counts as slower if the interval lies wholly above.

Stop and walk would replace the lazy kernel, everywhere lazy letters run now, if three things held. β = 1.5 had to be faster at one of those counts or more. It had to be slower at none. And its peak memory had to stay within 10% of the shipped kernel's at every count. Faster at some counts and slower at others is a finding, not an adoption. Stop and walk gets no thread range of its own, and moving the lazy threshold would be a separate decision. Because its verdict could change a default, the rule had one review before the run. The run also recorded two figures without judging them. One is how much slower each setting runs on one thread. The other is how much more processor time it takes at 10 threads than at 1, where a smaller working set should show.

The verdict: not adopted. Our reading of the run applied the rule's checker, frozen before the data, to the run's results. β = 1.5 ran slower at 8, 9 and 20 threads. At 10 and 12 we could not tell it from the shipped kernel. Its peak memory stayed within 3% of the shipped kernel's at every count, and the run's guard on a text corpus was inconclusive at every count. Wall time, stop and walk at β = 1.5 over the shipped lazy kernel, on production's plan of one worker a core:

Threads Wall time ratio 95% interval Reading 8 1.012 1.004 to 1.019 slower 9 1.010 1.004 to 1.016 slower 10 0.991 0.980 to 1.003 no difference detected 12 0.997 0.985 to 1.010 no difference detected 20 1.015 1.003 to 1.027 slower

What we learned. The memory relief is real. Going from 1 thread to 10, the shipped kernel's processor time grows, because the threads compete for the cache. Stop and walk's grows 5% less: its ratio of the two is 0.947 (0.913 to 0.982) of the shipped kernel's. But with one worker a core, that relief did not repay the walk. On one thread stop and walk ran 6.4% slower (1.064, 1.032 to 1.096), because each step of the walk waits for the one before. When we forced two workers onto each core, 12 or 20 of them, stop and walk ran faster: 0.986 of the shipped kernel's time at 12 workers and 0.965 at 20. mibz2's plan never puts two workers on a core of the i9, so that gain is out of reach.

What comes next. The cost to remove is the walk's serial wait. The open question is whether the walk can split into independent chains that overlap their waits, or whether the kernel can read the stopped map more cheaply. Until one of those exists, the test variants stay on their branch.

The chain, in short. The full rebuild holds its words to the end because it learns their places only in its last steps. Walking the small map left after an early stop learns the places another way. So the last fifth of the steps never run, and a third of the word bytes never get made. Putting the stop on an existing counter, and copying each word after its first expansion, keep the cost to about 11 or 12 instructions a letter. Since 0.5.1 the lazy kernel runs from 8 threads to 20 on the i9. So a memory cut to it reaches the whole range where threads contend for the cache. The timing said no: with one worker a core, the walk's waits cost more than the memory it saves. With two workers a core the relief showed, so a walk that overlaps its waits could still change the answer. Either way, mibz2 now has a second way to finish an induction, with a proof that it is correct and a kernel that gives the right bytes.
